articles.title: Sport's Strangest Crimes - Tennis' Darkest Hour - 2. There’s Always A Contender - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: There’s a new number one - but not everything is easy when you’re at the top.
articles.body:
Radio 5 Live , · 14 Sep 2026 , · 45 mins

Steffi Graf had been world number one for 3 years; it seemed like nobody could challenge her supremacy. But then along came a teenage girl from Yugoslavia, whose aggressive style - that came with grunting to match - challenged Graf’s dominance as well as the status quo. Finally, there was a contender. Clare Balding takes us through the most exciting moments in this emerging rivalry, as well as the darkness that swirled behind the scenes. How Seles’ record breaking was sidelined for her breaking of etiquette, and what it was like for young girls like her who found themselves in the very adult world of elite tennis in the 90s. In the age of the indomitable Steffi Graf, what made people think that Seles could be the greatest player the women’s game had ever seen? And what put both players on a collision course that would end with one of them in hospital? Presented by Clare Balding Produced by Emma Roberts Additional reporting by Russell Fuller Mixed by Gareth Isles Executive Producer: Joe Haddow Assistant Commissioner: Rob Green Commissioning Executive: Stevie Middleton

articles.title: What you need to know about the huge donations to Reform UK
articles.summary: Chief political correspondent Henry Zeffman explains who's behind Reform UK's £72m in donations.
articles.body:
Reform UK's Deputy Leader Richard Tice has said the government is trying to "retrospectively change the rules" on political donations, ahead of a debate on Monday in the House of Lords.

The party announced £72m in donations from two billionaires days before a bill that could introduce a £100,000 cap on donations from British voters living abroad returns to Parliament.

The huge donations, worth £36m each, came from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas. Reform UK says their donations would still be legal even under the proposed law change.

The BBC's chief political correspondent Henry Zeffman explains why the donations are controversial and what happens next.

articles.title: ‘I’m sick of her talking about it’: 11 readers share how GLP-1s have affected their relationships
articles.summary: As weight loss drugs have risen all around the world, it has reshaped users’ relationships for better and for worse
articles.body:
As GLP-1 use continues to rise in the US and the UK , people's bodies are being reshaped – as are their relationships.

"Relationships tend to develop a sense of equilibrium and predictability over time," says Dr Lindsey Berisha, a licensed clinical psychologist who has worked with clients using GLP-1s for over 10 years. "When one partner undergoes a significant change, it can shift that equilibrium, and even positive change can create uncertainty for both partners."

Berisha says that her clients who use GLP-1s often report feeling relieved that they are no longer consumed with thoughts of food. These users often develop more self-compassion , she says, as they realize what they previously interpreted as a failure or lack of self-control was a legitimate biological drive and food preoccupation that made life harder for them. "This shift can often be more impactful than the weight loss itself," she says.

But these changes can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends, says psychologist Dr Rachel Goldman, ranging "from being supportive to feeling insecure, left behind, or worried that the relationship itself is changing".

None of these reactions mean there is a problem with the medication or the relationship, Goldman emphasizes: "The goal is to recognize those shifts, communicate about them, and find new ways to connect rather than assuming the other person knows what you're experiencing."

Below, 11 Guardian readers share how GLP-1 use has shaped their relationships.

I can't share my experience with my unsupportive husband

My husband is unsupportive. He's afraid of long-term, currently unknown side-effects and likens GLP-1s to Fen-phen . As a result, I don't discuss my experience with him. This has been a life-changing drug so far, and I can't share it with the person I'm closest with. I can't share the wins, the way I'm amazed and thrilled with how I feel, and I certainly can't share any concerns or worries. It's contributed to a distance between us.

I've struggled with obesity for my entire adult life, and my family and personal health history put me at very high risk of dying young due to complications from the disease. But my husband scoffs at characterising obesity as a chronic and recurring disease. Instead, he thinks people should just make better lifestyle choices and stop making excuses – which tells me a lot about how he views me, too. – Anonymous

The biggest impact has been on my daughter

I have been on Wegovy for six months and have lost over two stone (28lb; 13kg). The biggest impact has been on my 20-year-old daughter. I didn't tell her I was on it and she found out when one of her friends went in the fridge and spotted it. I didn't deliberately hide it in the fridge, but I also didn't make it easy to find. We had discussed weight, identity and GLP-1s, but I was so ashamed of going on it that I didn't want to tell anyone.

My daughter felt worried, angry and jealous. Food is a huge part of our family life – when everyone is home, we cook together and eat together. What kind of signal am I giving her and her brothers? So much of my insecurity about my weight and appearance is offloaded on to an injectable pen. My husband hasn't really said much. He's observing me. He also wants to lose weight, but maybe not enough to intervene in that way. I'm the family guinea pig.

I feel conflicted but mostly positive. I am carrying less weight. My back doesn't hurt like it did. I can put on socks and shoes without being sore. I am more flexible. Calmer. I feel better. I care more about what I wear. I feel confident. I eat more healthily and drink less alcohol. The conflict comes in feeling like I'm cheating, like I don't have enough willpower or strength to lose weight independently. What I need to do is own it and say, "Fuck it, I feel so much better." But it's not that simple. – Anonymous

It makes me feel greedy and slightly envious

My partner takes GLP-1s. I'm glad he is losing weight and is happy in himself, though it's hard when we go out for a meal and have something to share. It makes me feel greedy. I feel slightly envious too, which is illogical. I would like to lose weight and am doing so without GLP-1s as I have a history of eating disorders and was recently pregnant but sadly miscarried. Maybe my partner being healthier will help us conceive.

I think GLP-1s are brilliant and can really help people. My partner has struggled [with weight loss] before and this seems to be working. I am concerned about people using it who don't need it, though. It's complicated. – Anonymous

I'm sick of her talking about nothing else

My best friend of 15 years has recently lost three stone (42lb; 19kg) after being on a GLP-1. I am pleased for her as she seems incredibly happy. Unfortunately, she regularly talks about food and weight now. She talks at length about how much weight she has lost, the old clothes she fits into, and how good everyone says she looks. I am pleased for her but sick of her talking about nothing else.

I have struggled with weight and food. I don't want to go on a GLP-1, but I am struggling even more being surrounded by people who are on it. I don't like how [these drugs] seem to be shifting the narrative around weight so that fatness is suddenly massively unacceptable again. – Anonymous

The truth is that [using] GLP-1s hasn't really affected my relationships at all. My partner knows about it but forgets all the time, because it's not changed our lives together. My friends don't know, but they don't know about my iron supplements either – what's that got to do with anything?

For me, my main issue is binge eating, which is a very private and isolating habit. Nobody I love saw me tear through three takeaways a night – I'd hide that, which would create a distancing sense of shame. If anything, the medication means I can be more present and open with the people I care about.

It's funny that people talk about GLP-1s being the "easy" way to lose weight. Yes! Isn't that the point? I got my first fillings at 23 and remember telling my dentist how amazing anaesthetic is. Yes, I could get a root canal without anaesthetic, or lose weight by white-knuckling hunger pangs and miserable restrictions. Or I could use the brilliant medical invention that makes reaching my health goal feel just fine. – Anonymous

I have pretended I don't care about being fat all my life

I have been on a GLP-1 for nearly two years and have kept it largely secret. Weight stigma is real. At work, people respect me more – people I don't know have more time for me, and I get more praise than before. It's ridiculous and so fucking rude.

Generally, my friends are really pleased for me. They have seen my weight fluctuate over the years. My concern is that I am still concealing my secret. I don't want people to think I've cheated. I guess there is still fat shame somewhere. I have pretended I don't care about being fat all my life. If I told people I was on this damn drug, they would know I was lying [about not caring]. I may tell them as time goes on. Some will have guessed. It's the wild west out here, in social terms.

My partner is really happy for me. She loves that I look fire so much these days, and that is partly because I can dress well. I think she has felt insecure at times because of my glow-up. But that is only one thing. It doesn't change our combined life, our shared ambitions and understanding. – Anonymous

I love myself for the first time in a long time

As soon as I lost 5 stone (70lb; 32kg), my husband told me he's no longer in love with me. It totally floored me. I knew that I had become the woman I wanted to be, but I was no longer the woman who needed his validation.

After a lot of heartache, I decided to stay and fix whatever broke between us. We have been together for 32 years, married for 25; we have three children and a beautiful home. We are trying to be the best for each other and have started dating again. There is still no intimacy, but the love and respect are there.

I love myself for the first time in such a long, long time. I only want the best for me. – Anonymous

I have been using a GLP-1 for two years and have lost nearly ⅓ of my former body weight. Almost nobody in my life knows. I have family members and close friends who have used them and have been open about it. I really admire their ability to be so honest with everyone. I feel like I am being dishonest with people even though I don't ever deny using them – I just don't offer the information.

I've started a new relationship and my partner doesn't know. I like to think he would be with me regardless of my weight. I think the main difference in myself that led to the relationship is my confidence and my willingness to put myself out there. Maybe one day I will tell him, but not yet. – Anonymous

My ex-wife started using them to lose weight a few years ago. After about a year, she had lost 70lb (31.8kg). I was super proud and excited for her. But then she left me for another guy and now I'm divorced. – Anonymous

The drug not only destroyed any appetite that my wife had, but it destroyed any desire she had for anything other than sitting around watching TV. My wife used to be a little chubby, but she was happy and we had a good life. Now she says she is "skinny, ugly and hates [herself]". – Anonymous

If he hadn't been supportive, it would have been much harder

I've lost 35kg (77.2 lb) on Mounjaro, which I started in December 2024. I've maintained my weight loss on a micro-dose for almost a year. I feel calmer, more confident, and much more inclined to initiate sex. I've lost my appetite for greasy, heavy foods, and probably still eat under half of what I used to. This was hard on my foodie partner, but he knew how important it was for me to achieve a healthy weight.

I started exercising daily, and now my husband has joined me. Now, instead of drinking wine and eating cheese together, we go to the pool or the hot springs, and on evenings and weekends we walk. If he hadn't been supportive and willing to join me on my health journey, it would've been much harder. – Sara, 42, Brunswick, UK

articles.title: Seis dias de chuva afetam mais de 14 mil pessoas, interditam rodovias e deixam cidade do Paraná praticamente isolada | G1
articles.standfirst: Balanço da Defesa Civil reúne ocorrências registradas desde quarta-feira (9) em 60 municípios. Adrianópolis, na Grande Curitiba, está sem água e energia após erosão interditar trecho da BR-476.
articles.summary: Balanço da Defesa Civil reúne ocorrências registradas desde quarta-feira (9) em 60 municípios.
articles.body:
As chuvas que atingem o Paraná desde quarta-feira (9) deixaram 14.675 pessoas afetadas em 60 municípios , segundo balanço da Defesa Civil atualizado às 5h30 desta segunda-feira (14).

No período, foram registradas 67 ocorrências, com 2.073 pessoas desalojadas, 395 desabrigadas e três mortes. Também foram contabilizadas 2.680 casas danificadas e uma destruída.

Entre as cidades mais afetadas está Adrianópolis , no Região Metropolitana de Curitiba , que está sem acesso pela BR-476 depois que uma erosão provocada pela chuva fez parte do asfalto desabar, no km 6.

Equipes conseguiram chegar à cidade por uma rota liberada apenas para veículos 4x4, mas o caminho está em condições precárias e é considerado perigoso, segundo a Secretaria da Segurança Pública do Paraná (Sesp). O relatório da Defesa Civil registra 112 pessoas afetadas e duas desalojadas.

A cidade está sem energia elétrica e sem água, segundo as informações apuradas pela equipe. A Unidade de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) funciona com gerador.

Erosão faz asfalto 'desabar' e deixa cidade isolada no Paraná — Foto: PRF

Na região do Vale do Ribeira, Tunas do Paraná também registrou vários deslizamentos. Equipes do Departamento Nacional de Infraestrutura de Transportes (DNIT) trabalham na retirada das barreiras que atingiram a pista.

Na região do Jardim das Oliveiras, em Almirante Tamandaré , moradores da Rua Ernestina Pereira da Silva foram orientados pela Defesa Civil a deixar as casas por causa do risco de novos deslizamentos. Um grande volume de terra desceu pela área e levou um poste, deixando moradores sem energia.

Segundo a Defesa Civil do município, 30 famílias foram realocadas para casas de familiares. Um vídeo também mostra parte de uma casa despencando. Ninguém ficou ferido.

Queda de barreira e poste em Tunas do Paraná — Foto: SESP

Em Rio Branco do Sul , o balanço estadual aponta 72 pessoas afetadas, oito desalojadas e 18 casas danificadas. Segundo a Defesa Civil, dois rapazes teriam caído na correnteza de um rio e seguem desaparecidos . As buscas serão retomadas nesta segunda-feira (14).

São José dos Pinhais registrou 320 pessoas afetadas, 20 desalojadas e 72 casas danificadas.

Em Araucária , são 220 pessoas afetadas considerando as ocorrências de inundação e alagamento registradas no período. O município também contabiliza 63 desabrigados e 40 casas danificadas.

Na PR-092, há quedas de barreira, desmoronamentos e galhos entre Jaguariaíva e Doutor Ulysses , mas o trânsito flui. Entre Doutor Ulysses e Cerro Azul , o trecho está interditado, com desvio. Já a PR-340, entre Cerro Azul e Tunas do Paraná, está bloqueada.

articles.title: Tartarugas acasalam e ganham ‘plateia’ de golfinhos em Noronha | G1
articles.standfirst: Fotógrafo Lito Noronha registrou a cena com drone na Praia do Americano. Segundo pesquisadores, golfinhos-rotadores podem ter ficado curiosos com o comportamento das tartarugas.
articles.summary: Fotógrafo Lito Noronha registrou a cena com drone na Praia do Americano.  Segundo pesquisadores, golfinhos-rotadores podem ter ficado curiosos com o comportamento das tartarugas.
articles.body:
Em um voo de drone, o fotógrafo Carlos Eduardo Ferreira da Silva, conhecido como Lito Noronha, registrou uma cena curiosa na Praia do Americano, em Fernando de Noronha . Duas tartarugas-verdes aparecem acasalando, enquanto uma terceira tartaruga e um grupo de golfinhos-rotadores observam a cena. O registro chamou a atenção pela interação entre as espécies ( veja vídeo acima ).

“Resolvi produzir imagens logo cedo e percebi que os golfinhos estavam interagidos com o acasalamento das tartarugas, foi curioso, bem raro”, contou Lito.

Tartarugas copulam e golfinhos observam em Noronha — Foto: Lito Noronha/Acervo pessoal

As tartarugas são da espécie verde ( Chelonia mydas ). O geógrafo Renan Louzada, agente ambiental do Centro Tamar, avaliou o registro.

“Achei fantástico o registro, muito legal a interação dos golfinhos com as tartarugas. Nós identificamos uma fêmea e dois machos no ato de reprodução. Um macho copula enquanto o outro está no aguardo. Esse é um comportamento comum. Às vezes, ocorre de uma fêmea copular com cinco machos ao redor. Eles disputam espaço para o ato sexual na sequência”, falou o pesquisador.

Renan Louzada explicou que as tartarugas-verdes da imagem têm pouco mais de um metro de comprimento de casco, o que indica que são adultas. Ele também comentou a interação entre as espécies registrada.

“A interação entre golfinhos-rotadores e tartarugas-verdes é algo que o oceano pode proporcionar. Apesar de não ser especialista em golfinhos, acredito que eles estavam curiosos para ver o que se passava”, falou Renan.

A imagem foi enviada para o Programa Ciência Cidadã do Projeto Golfinho Rotador, intitulado “Acho que Vi um Golfinho”.

O oceanógrafo José Martins, coordenador do projeto, explicou que o comportamento dos golfinhos pode ser interpretado como uma forma de investigação. Segundo ele, os animais que passavam pelo local podem ter ficado curiosos com a cena.

“O comportamento de golfinhos-rotadores cercarem grupos de cópula de tartarugas-verdes já tinha sido observado anteriormente, mas nunca tínhamos conseguido registros com a qualidade das imagens feitas pelo fotógrafo profissional Lito Noronha”, contou Martins.

Além da importância ambiental do registro, o oceanógrafo destacou que Lito Noronha, de 37 anos, já havia trabalhado como estagiário no Projeto Golfinho Rotador quando tinha 17 anos.

O pesquisador também destacou a importância da colaboração de moradores e visitantes para ampliar os registros de animais marinhos na ilha.

“O Projeto Golfinho Rotador quer ampliar o banco de dados colaborativo sobre golfinhos e baleias em Fernando de Noronha, ao mesmo tempo que aproximamos ilhéus e visitantes desses animais tão importantes para Noronha. É uma ótima oportunidade de incentivar a observação de cetáceos, estimulando o aprendizado e a valorização dos mamíferos marinhos e aumentando a conexão com as espécies locais”, informou José Martins.

Os interessados em participar podem preencher o formulário d o programa.

Criado em 1990, o Projeto Golfinho Rotador realiza pesquisas e ações de conservação dos golfinhos em Fernando de Noronha, com apoio do Programa Petrobras Socioambiental. A organização também promove oficinas culturais, incentiva o surfe entre jovens e desenvolve atividades educativas nas duas escolas da ilha.

articles.title: UE acusa Rússia de atacar trem após passagem autoridades europeias | G1
articles.standfirst: Trem que levava ex-premiê Boris Johnson e outros diplomatas europeus passou por estação de Yahodyn, a 2 km do território polonês, pouco antes de drone a jato atingir o local.
articles.summary: Trem que levava ex-premiê Boris Johnson e outros diplomatas europeus passou por estação de Yahodyn, a 2 km do território polonês, pouco antes de drone a jato atingir o local.
articles.body:
Um drone russo atingiu uma estação ferroviária na fronteira entre a Ucrânia e a Polônia no domingo (13) momentos após a passagem de um trem levando autoridades diplomáticas europeias de alto escalão.

O projétil atingiu um trem na estação ucraniana de Yahodyn, que fica a dois quilômetros da fronteira com a Polônia. O vagão foi evacuado apenas minutos antes, e não houve registro de feridos. A estação fica em uma rota frequentemente usada por delegações estrangeiras que vão à capital ucraniana Kiev por terra.

O ataque aéreo ocorreu pouco após a passagem de um trem que levava diversas autoridades europeias , como o ex-premiê britânico Boris Johnson, o ex-premiê sueco Carl Bildt e o conselheiro de Segurança Nacional do Reino Unido, Jonathan Powell. Eles faziam o trajeto entre as cidades de Kovel, na Ucrânia, e Dorohusk, na Polônia, após participarem de uma conferência de segurança em Kiev (veja no mapa abaixo) .

Mapa mostra localização de estação de Yahodyn, no extremo oeste da Ucrânia, alvo de ataque de drone russo em 13 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Dhara Pereira/Arte g1

A Ucrânia e a União Europeia acusaram a Rússia pelo incidente e disseram acreditar que o trem diplomático seria de fato o alvo dos russos. Isso porque o trem em que as autoridades europeias estavam teve seu cronograma acelerado por conta da "ameaça russa" e deixou Yahodyn mais cedo que o planejado. Se não fosse o caso, o veículo poderia ter sido atingido, segundo Kiev.

“É perfeitamente possível que o alvo pretendido pelo drone russo fosse o trem diplomático, que deixou a estação mais cedo do que o previsto depois que os horários dos trens foram ajustados em tempo real devido à ameaça constante de ataques russos”, disse a operadora ferroviária ucraniana, Ukrzaliznytsia, no Telegram.

Bombeiros combatem incêndio em trem de passageiros atingido por drone russo em estação ferroviária em 13 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Serviço de Emergência de Volyn via Reuters

Perguntado sobre o incidente em coletiva nesta segunda, o porta-voz do Kremlin, Dmitry Peskov, disse apenas que "nossas forças militares estão operando em todo o território da Ucrânia e continuarão a fazê-lo". No domingo, a Rússia afirmou que atingiu “infraestruturas ferroviárias” no oeste ucraniano utilizadas para transportar carga militar proveniente da Europa.

Boris Johnson condenou o ataque, que chamou de “aleatório e sem sentido”. O ex-chefe da CIA David Petraeus, que estava a bordo de outro trem que estava parado na estação de Yahodyn no momento do ataque, disse que o incidente foi "aterrorizante" e chamou o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, de "bárbaro".

Também no domingo, um caminhão a menos de um quilômetro da fronteira da Ucrânia com a Polônia também foi atingido, levando o posto de fronteira de Dorohusk-Yahodyn a interromper temporariamente as operações, segundo os guardas de fronteira.

articles.title: Irã e Houthis: Teerã nega participação em conflito no Iêmen | G1
articles.standfirst: Nesta segunda, a Defesa Civil saudita emitiu alertas de perigo em quatro cidades do sul do país. O porta-voz militar do grupo extremista anunciou ter atacado a Base Aérea Rei Khalid.
articles.summary: Nesta segunda, a Defesa Civil da Arábia Saudita emitiu alertas de perigo em quatro cidades do sul do país. O porta-voz militar dos Houthis anunciou ter atacado base aérea saudita.
articles.body:
O Irã negou, nesta segunda-feira (14), qualquer envolvimento no conflito travado pelos Houthis, grupo extremista do Iêmen que é aliado do regime, com as forças governamentais iemenitas e a Arábia Saudita.

Em declaração à imprensa, o porta-voz do Ministério das Relações Exteriores iraniano, Esmaeil Baqaei, afirmou que os houthis são "totalmente independentes" e "tomam suas decisões em função de seus próprios interesses".

"O Irã não interfere nos assuntos iemenitas", declarou, anunciando ainda que o governo saudita solicitou o adiamento de uma reunião entre Teerã e as potências do Golfo para apresentar um acordo com Omã sobre a regulamentação das rotas marítimas pelo Estreito de Ormuz.

➡️ Os houthis, que controlam as áreas mais populosas do Iêmen e grande parte do norte do país, vêm lançando ataques contra a Arábia Saudita desde que declararam um bloqueio naval contra Riad em julho, com ataques direcionados a navios sauditas no Mar Vermelho.

Nesta segunda, a Defesa Civil saudita emitiu alertas de perigo em quatro cidades do sul do país. O porta-voz militar do grupo extremista anunciou ter ter atacado a Base Aérea Rei Khalid , em Khamis Mushait, a quinta maior cidade da Arábia Saudita, visando instalações e infraestrutura militar

Esmaeil Baqaei, porta-voz do Ministério das Relações Exteriores do Irã — Foto: REUTERS

O porta-voz da chancelaria iraniana também protestou contra uma decisão da Áustria que impediu o chefe do setor nuclear do Irã, Mohamad Eslami, de participar de uma conferência anual na sede da agência de energia atômica da ONU em Viena.

Ele classificou a medida do governo austríaco de "totalmente injustificável" e a creditou à pressão dos Estados Unidos:

"É evidente para todos nós que este incidente aconteceu devido às pressões dos Estados Unidos, mas isso não exonera o governo austríaco de toda responsabilidade".

Navio navega no Estreito de Bab el-Mandeb em abril de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Na sexta-feira (11), os Houthis chegaram à cidade portuária de Dhubab e à ilha de Perim, ambas no sudoeste do Iêmen e na região do Estreito de Bab el-Mandeb, e ficaram mais próximos de controlar o acesso ao Mar Vermelho .

A movimentação marcou o avanço mais significativo do grupo terrorista iemenita até o momento rumo ao Estreito de Bab el-Mandeb, segundo a agência de notícias. Controlar Dhubab e Perim é vital para controlar o a via marítima, que é uma das mais importantes do mundo por ligar o Mar Vermelho ao Hemisfério Oriental, de acordo com as fontes do governo do Iêmen.

Na quinta-feira, os Houthis já haviam tomado Moca . Apesar dos avanços, o grupo terrorista iemenita disse nesta sexta que o tráfego por el-Mandeb, segunda rota mais importante para o comércio de petróleo, permanecia seguro e ininterrupto.

“A liberdade de navegação e o comércio internacional no Mar Vermelho e em Bab al-Mandab estão seguros e sob controle. (...) Não há motivo para preocupação internacional, pois eles não enfrentam nenhum perigo vindo do lado iemenita”, disse Hazem al-Assad, membro do bureau político Houthi.

Atualmente, os Houthis travam uma guerra civil contra as forças governamentais do Iêmen, e esse conflito reaqueceu nos últimos meses por conta da guerra do Oriente Médio, que apesar de ser entre EUA, Irã e Israel incitou outros focos de combates pela região. Ao menos 46 mil pessoas fugiram no Iêmen em meio à escalada dos combates no país, segundo a ONU.

Quando o grupo extremista anunciou um bloqueio marítimo contra a Arábia Saudita , fontes de agências de notícia afirmaram que a decisão ocorreu após um pedido do Irã, aliado dos houthis, para que eles atuassem no Estreito de Bab el-Mandeb.

articles.title: Primeira missa inclusiva do RS acolhe famílias atípicas | G1
articles.standfirst: Celebração na Paróquia Sagrado Coração de Jesus, em Montenegro, permitiu livre circulação para receber fiéis com sensibilidade sensorial e evitar o julgamento social.
articles.summary: Celebração na Paróquia Sagrado Coração de Jesus, em Montenegro, permitiu livre circulação para receber fiéis com sensibilidade sensorial e evitar o julgamento social
articles.body:
A Diocese de Montenegro , município a 60 quilômetros de Porto Alegre , realizou neste domingo (13) a primeira missa inclusiva do Rio Grande do Sul . A celebração, ocorrida na Paróquia Sagrado Coração de Jesus, foi adaptada para acolher pessoas atípicas e suas famílias, minimizando barreiras sensoriais e sociais .

Para o vigário da paróquia, Oséias Dreyer, a adaptação reforça o papel de acolhimento da comunidade. "A vida nasce como um dom precioso. Não sou eu e nem o outro que pode desqualificar a importância e a beleza que cada ser humano traz dentro de si, que é o amor de Deus", destaca.

Para atender às necessidades do público, a organização reduziu o volume do som e utilizou iluminação suave . A cerimônia contou com intérprete de língua de sinais e os participantes tiveram liberdade para levantar e caminhar pelo espaço durante o rito.

A rotina das missas tradicionais costuma afastar famílias de crianças atípicas devido ao incômodo com ruídos e ao julgamento de terceiros. Mãe de Elias, a dona de casa Michele Regina Machado relata a dificuldade.

"Eu como mãe, eu posso dizer que por muito tempo eu fiquei afastada da igreja. Eu trazia meu filho quando ele era pequeno, mas ele fazia muitos barulhos, estereotipias, isso incomodava as pessoas", afirma.

Durante a missa, Elias, que possui sensibilidade ao toque e não consegue usar camisa e sapatos, acompanhou o início da celebração do lado de fora.

O pai, Odirlei Bernardes, relatou estar feliz mesmo acompanhando a missa da rua . "O pouquinho que ele puder vir aqui, estar sentindo um pouco desta atmosfera, para nós é de grande valia."

Na sequência, Elias conseguiu entrar na igreja. A mãe emocionou-se com o momento.

"Ele não usa camiseta e calçado há quatro anos, então eu não consigo levar nos lugares. Ver ele entrando na casa do Senhor agora me causou uma emoção muito grande como mãe poder trazer meu filho na igreja. Nós pais que estamos aqui, a gente sabe o quão difícil é a gente levar nossos filhos para a sociedade", relata.

O vigário ressalta que a iniciativa busca oferecer um ambiente sem julgamentos , pois os pais costumam se preocupar.

"Nós como comunidade queremos justamente dizer a elas que a preocupação maior delas, ou o pensamento melhor delas, pode ser: vamos para a igreja para que lá nos encontramos paz", declara o religioso.

As crianças presentes aproveitaram a liberdade de movimento. Francisco dos Santos, de nove anos, resumiu a experiência: "Eu tô me sentindo muito bem".

articles.title: Chuva em Santos supera o dobro da média histórica de setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: A Defesa Civil Estadual informou que a Baixada Santista lidera o acumulado de chuva em todo o estado de São Paulo nas últimas 12 horas.
articles.summary: A Defesa Civil Estadual informou que a Baixada Santista lidera o acumulado de chuva em todo o estado de São Paulo nas últimas 12 horas.
articles.body:
Avenida Nossa Senhora de Fátima registra alagamento em Santos — Foto: Prefeitura de Santos

O volume de chuva em Santos , no litoral de São Paulo, chegou a 400,99 milímetros nas duas primeiras semanas de setembro. O índice registrado em apenas duas semanas já supera o dobro da média histórica para todo o mês na cidade.

De acordo com a Prefeitura de Santos, a média histórica de setembro dos últimos 25 anos é de 139,9 mm. O número, porém, já foi quase igualado nas últimas 72h, quando foi registrado o volume de 132,39 mm na cidade.

A Defesa Civil Estadual informou que a Baixada Santista liderava o acumulado de chuva em todo o estado de São Paulo nas últimas 12 horas. Segundo o balanço do órgão estadual, divulgado às 6h20, o maior volume foi registrado em Cubatão com 45 milímetros, seguido por Praia Grande (39 mm), Guarujá (38 mm), Mongaguá (38 mm), Santos (37 mm) e São Vicente (35 mm).

Em Santos, os morros estão em estado de atenção. Segundo a prefeitura, a queda de uma árvore no bairro Vila Mathias causou bloqueio no canal 1 (Avenida Senador Pinheiro Machado), no sentido praia/Centro. Desta forma, o trânsito está sendo desviado para a Rua Lucas Fortunato nesta segunda-feira (14).

A Companhia de Engenharia de Tráfego (CET-Santos) informou que a Avenida Nossa Senhora de Fátima apresenta pontos de alagamentos em ambos os sentidos, em todas as faixas, nas proximidades da Rua Ana Santos.

Apesar disso, a administração municipal informou que a faixa da esquerda está transitável nos dois sentidos para veículos de pequeno porte.

A Prefeitura de Mongaguá informou que, no fim de semana, houve um acionamento da Defesa Civil para atendimento de uma família no bairro Itaguaí. Segundo a administração, os moradores chegaram a ser orientados sobre a possibilidade de acolhimento em local disponibilizado pela prefeitura, mas optaram por permanecer na residência após o escoamento das águas.

O acumulado de chuva na cidade foi de 109 mm em 72 horas. No período de 48 horas, foram registrados 68 mm, e, nas últimas 24 horas, 51 mm. A Defesa Civil permanece acompanhando a situação e não foi acionada para outras ocorrências no município.

Em São Vicente, um morador registrou a Avenida Salgado Filho, no bairro Jóquei, completamente alagada. Alguns veículos encararam a água na metade do pneu para atravessar a via ( veja abaixo ).

Avenida Salgado Filho, no bairro Jóquei, ficou alagada em São Vicente — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Sérgio Domingos da Silva

Em nota, a Prefeitura de São Vicente informou que não registrou ocorrências, apenas pontos de alagamento transitáveis:

Avenida Augusto Severo, próximo à Avenida Galeão Coutinho;

Avenida Augusto Severo, próximo à Rua Indaiatuba.

Segundo a administração municipal, as forças de segurança permanecem mobilizadas para eventuais ocorrências, com equipes acompanhando as condições climáticas e prestando atendimento à população.

A Prefeitura de Peruíbe disse que uma árvore caiu na região da Prainha no sábado (12).

Bertioga e Itanhaém informaram que não registraram ocorrências.

articles.title: Tomate, açúcar e óleo puxam queda de 4%¨da cesta básica no Acre | G1
articles.standfirst: Média chegou a R$ 659,66 em agosto deste ano na capital. Levantamento tem como base preços de produtos considerando a necessidade mensal das famílias.
articles.summary: Média chegou a R$ 659,66 em agosto deste ano na capital. Levantamento tem como base preços de produtos considerando a necessidade mensal das famílias.
articles.body:
🛒🍅O custo da cesta básica em Rio Branco teve queda de 4,6% entre julho e agosto, e chegou a R$ 659,66 no oitavo mês deste ano. É o que aponta uma pesquisa do Departamento Intersindical de Estatística e Estudos Socioeconômicos (Dieese).

Conforme o balanço, a redução no bolso do consumidor acreano foi puxada principalmente pela queda nos preços do tomate (25,93%), açúcar cristal (2,94%) e do óleo de soja (1,34%) . Além disso, Rio Branco ocupou a 7ª posição entre os valores mais baratos do país.

Segundo o Dieese, a capital acreana ficou atrás apenas de Aracaju (R$ 570,98), Natal (R$ 627,42), Maceió (R$ 627,45), Salvador (R$ 628,89), João Pessoa (R$ 641,13) e Recife (R$ 643,02), que teve a cesta básica mais barata do país no mês de agosto.

Entre as capitais com o custo da cesta básica mais cara, lideram São Paulo , com R$ 900,59 , Cuiabá , que teve R$ 851,57 e Rio de Janeiro , com R$ 851,19 . Em comparação ao estado paulista, a diferença para o valor da cesta no Acre é de 26,7%.

Custo da cesta básica em Rio Branco recuou 4,6% em agosto, chegando a R$ 659,66 — Foto: Alex Ferreira

Além dos três principais itens que ajudaram na queda, outros alimentos que compõem a cesta também registraram baixa em seus preços na capital do Acre, contudo, com bem menos impacto na hora de pagar:

Por outro lado, a queda no valor total não foi ainda maior porque seis dos 12 produtos pesquisados ficaram mais caros no período. As maiores altas foram lideradas pela farinha de mandioca, que subiu 8,93%, o arroz tipo agulhinha, 3,45%, e manteiga, 2,10%.

Também registraram aumento o leite integral, 0,79%, a banana, 0,69%, e a carne bovina de primeira, 0,33%. O custo da alimentação básica em Rio Branco acumula alta de 2,87% nos últimos 12 meses.

Em agosto de 2026, o trabalhador de Rio Branco precisou trabalhar por 89 horas e 32 minutos, ou, aproximadamente, 11 dias, para conseguir comprar a cesta. O tempo ainda foi menor do que as 93 horas e 55 minutos observadas em julho.

Em termos financeiros, a compra da cesta comprometeu 43,9% do salário mínimo líquido (após o desconto de 7,5% da Previdência Social), houve uma melhora em relação aos 46,15% registrados no mês anterior.

A pesquisa da Dieese com a Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), em supermercados da capital, avaliou 12 alimentos considerados como necessidade mensal de famílias com até três adultos ou dois adultos e duas crianças.

Os produtos analidados foram: tomate, açúcar cristal, óleo de soja, feijão carioca, café em pó, pão francês, farinha de mandioca, arroz agulhinha, manteiga, leite integral, banana e a carne bovina de primeira, que são os cortes mais macios como a picanha, alcatra e o filé mignon.

Além disso, segundo uma pesquisa do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), divulgada em agosto, a média de R$ 3.149 no rendimento mensal per capita no estado , deixou o Acre com o terceiro maior da região Norte, o valor impacta diretamente na compra de insumos básicos.

articles.title: Restored Cheshire wetland becomes haven for rare birds
articles.summary: Woolston Eyes, near Warrington, is home to the largest black-necked grebe population in the UK.
articles.body:
A restored wetland in Cheshire is now home to almost two-thirds of the UK's breeding black-necked grebes, one of the country's rarest breeding birds.

Woolston Eyes, near Warrington, was previously a dumping ground for dredging from the Manchester Ship Canal. It is now the site of the country's largest colony of the species.

Black-necked grebes are known for their distinctive golden facial tufts and average about 55 breeding pairs in the UK each year, according to the RSPB .

"It is fantastic to see black-necked grebe numbers increasing at Woolston Eyes," RSPB ecologist Gavin Thomas said. "The rapid growth in numbers shows how effective targeted conservation action can be."

Since 2021, Woolston Eyes has been transformed from a former dredging site into a network of freshwater pools and reedbeds.

Black-necked grebes were already breeding on a nearby wetland when four pairs nested on the newly restored site in 2023, successfully raising 15 young.

By 2025, the RSPB had recorded 35 breeding pairs across the reserve - with 29 nesting in the newly restored wetland area.

Robin Horner, from the RSPB, described the growth in numbers as "pretty amazing".

"This spring they had over 60 birds present on site," he said.

"It doesn't sound a lot but when you consider how scarce it is in the UK it's pretty amazing.

"It's one of those real success stories where industry and wildlife can actually work together."

articles.title: Photo call or 'pivotal moment' - How significant is leaders summit?
articles.summary: The first minister will meet the leaders of Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein in Cardiff on Monday.
articles.body:
John Swinney has claimed the UK is at a "pivotal moment of constitutional change" - ahead of a summit with the leaders of Plaid Cymru and Sinn Fein in Cardiff.

Swinney, Plaid's leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Sinn Féin's president Mary Lou McDonald and vice-president Michelle O'Neill, will discuss how the parties can work together on their shared interests.

The gathering marks the fact that, for the first time, the three devolved governments are represented by three nationalist first ministers (although O'Neill represents one half of Stormont's power-sharing administration).

All three seem keen to exploit this new political dynamic. But the question is, how exactly?

After all, when you dig beneath the surface of their shared goal of leaving the UK, the circumstances facing them look very different indeed.

Swinney is pushing for a second vote on independence following his win in May's Scottish elections.

First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff

In Wales, ap Iorwerth - who leads the Senedd's first pro-independence administration - is in less of a rush for a referendum, previously ruling one out for this parliament, and instead focusing on the devolution of more powers.

Speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg , ap Iorweth acknowledged the differing contexts.

"We have distinct nations with our own trajectories and our own priorities," he said.

"But there is also something that ties us together...that pursuit of a different attitude from UK government.

"It could be around the constitutional question, it could, more acutely, be around fair funding."

In Northern Ireland, there is already an agreed path to reunification as set out in the Good Friday Agreement.

That question of the devolved funding settlement is expected to be discussed, alongside other ways of working together in areas such as the economy and energy.

But perhaps the biggest opportunity for the nationalist leaders lies in the political rather than the practical.

Speaking ahead of the meeting, Swinney said: "For the first time ever, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are led by pro-independence first ministers.

"There could be no clearer sign that the status quo is not sustainable – and that Westminster must prepare for a post-UK future."

O'Neill echoed those sentiments, describing it as a "clear indication that people see that Westminster is not working for the people of the North, Scotland or Wales".

A photo-op featuring three nationalist first ministers is certainly a very visible reminder of the recent shift in the UK's political landscape - "good optics" as they say.

And the prospect of the trio of parties signing up to a shared agreement - aimed at putting pressure on Downing Street to plan and prepare for referendums - is a media spectacle, even though it carries no real weight.

The timing of this summit is also a gift for the SNP.

At last week's PMQs, Andy Burnham seemed to accept a parallel with Northern Ireland that if, and when, support for constitutional change reaches a certain level, a referendum in Scotland could be considered .

Downing Street has since rowed back, but as one SNP figure puts it, "the cat is well and truly out the bag".

Swinney is now seeking an agreed mechanism for triggering a vote, and his aides believe events like this one in Cardiff can help build both support and momentum.

Meanwhile, President Trump's remarks in support of Irish reunification have ensured the UK's constitutional arrangements remain firmly near the top of the news agenda.

That could feel like a "momentum changer" to Irish nationalists , according to the BBC's Northern Ireland political editor Enda McClafferty.

Of course, today's meeting of minds is not without risks.

The SNP and Plaid Cymru have a history as allies, but Swinney has faced criticism over his approach to working with Sinn Féin.

The shadow Scottish secretary Harriet Cross has described it as "a performative photo call" and a "distraction", adding that Swinney "should be spending time focusing on what really matters to Scots".

And there are some in his own ranks who believe talk of a referendum should be put on the back burner in favour of driving up support for independence.

With polling indicating Scots are evenly split over the constitutional question, that remains Swinney's biggest challenge.

articles.title: How this summer may have been when climate change felt real
articles.summary: This summer has seen hot weather records broken, drought and major damage from fires.
articles.body:
Is this the year climate change became real for people of the Midlands?

I mean climate change is real, I've spent a 25-year career telling people it is real and documenting its impact on the region: Floods, dry spells, heatwaves and more.

So why for many people does this year feel different - like climate change is finally "here" ?

Well in 2026, things have reached some sort of tipping point where we can start to see really obvious signs of change that had a huge impact on at least some of us.

A winter of endless rain, not just wet but never ending .

Then the rain stopped and we were hurtling into drought .

We have had wildfires this year because things have been so dry for so long, the hot air has just sucked the moisture out of the landscape.

It leaves vegetation dead, dry and needing just a small spark to erupt into flame.

On Cannock Chase, I spent the day with Staffordshire County Council rangers, as they showed me around the black, scorched earth left behind after the fires that took place there.

I saw pictures of dead adders along with cracked and burnt eggs belonging to ground-nesting birds.

It is not just wildlife affected by them - the ash from the fire is changing the chemistry of the soil itself.

It is much more nutrient-rich and that is bad news for this rare lowland heathland, where the traditional plants prefer poorer quality soil.

Already green shoots of bracken are bursting through the blackened earth and that will crowd out the traditional heather, bilberry and cowberry.

The Met Office has a list of things climate change will make worse, including "increased risk of fires" but it also says the "habitable region of pests expands".

That is exactly what our farmers are seeing this year.

Bluetongue is an awful disease affecting cattle and sheep, leading to the death of lambs and calves.

It is carried by infected midges and as the climate has warmed the region, infected midges have expanded north from Europe to now include the Midlands.

There were also nine cases in Shropshire, two in Herefordshire and one each in Worcestershire, Warwickshire and Solihull.

Thanks to climate change, farmers must now rethink the way they look after these animals, keep them inside when the risk is high, or consider spending money on vaccination.

Back at Cannock Chase, the small team is working to try and restore the charred landscape and also improve fire breaks and access for fire engines for when the next wildfire season starts.

Meanwhile "risk to water supplies" is another climate change issue identified by the Met Office, and Severn Trent is working to tackle that.

Not least by increasing the size of Draycote Water reservoir by 60cm (24 inches) so it can hold more water.

Everywhere you look in the region, people are dealing with the identified issues climate change is causing and it's costing all of us money.

Since we continue to keep pouring climate change gases into the environment the problems just keep increasing.

As one expert told me, climate change is here, the climate the UK was designed for no longer exists and that leaves us with no choice but to adapt.

Was this the year climate change finally felt "real" to you? Just wait until next year and the year after that.

articles.title: 'What's for dinner?' makes Birmingham couple TikTok and Instagram stars
articles.summary: Dawn Emmett films her partner Neil Haycock as he serves up their evening meals.
articles.body:
A couple have attracted millions of views on social media with videos built around a simple daily question: "What's for dinner?"

For the past seven months, Dawn Emmett has been filming her partner Neil Haycock as he serves up their evening meals at their home in Great Barr, Birmingham.

What started as a bit of fun has begun to appeal to TikTok, Instagram and Facebook users of all ages from around the world.

"We are so thankful for everyone being so kind, because we are older you don't know how it is going to go," Emmett said.

It started one night when the 58-year-old was scrolling through TikTok and started filming her partner cooking mussels and chips.

She posted it online, and a few days later thousands of people had viewed it, prompting her to continue uploading videos of her asking: "What's for dinner, Neil?

"It just snowballed and snowballed," she said. "It was 2,000 people, 10,000 people and then it was, 'oh my God we have got to a million views'."

For 53-year-old Haycock, cooking is something he has loved doing since he was a teenager.

"Mum brought me a Ken Hom cookbook and I got a passion for it," he said.

"I have always cooked, always cooked Sunday dinners. I find it really therapeutic and enjoyable."

One of his tasty-looking dishes has done particularly well online.

"I think the best one was when I did roast seabass on the barbecue and it came out with the whole fish with the head on, that was on about three-and-a-half million," Haycock said.

Millions have also watched him presenting his partner with a plate of peri-peri chicken with spicy rice, and another of pork belly with spiced red cabbage and fondant potatoes.

The videos have led to the couple gaining thousands of followers and even getting recognised locally.

Emmett said she had been out recently and a young girl had asked her if she was on TikTok.

articles.title: Buyer's note helped secure 'top six' holiday home near Stafford
articles.summary: Ben Harrison has spent £300,000 renovating a grade-II listed building in Tixall for rent on Airbnb.
articles.body:
A man whose holiday rental has been ranked among the best in the country said a personal note was the key to securing it six years ago.

Ben Harrison, has spent £300,000 renovating The Bottle Lodge, a 200-year-old, grade-II listed building in Tixall, near Stafford, Staffordshire.

The venue was recently named one of Hello Magazine's top six Airbnb cottages, which Harrison put down to its unusual octagonal shape.

"I think what we've done with the property is to try to keep its character as much as possible," he said.

"When we moved in there was a suspended ceiling upstairs [and] you couldn't see the dome.

"The first thing we wanted to do was basically build a frame within the roof that followed the shape of the roof, so when you walk upstairs and you look up you can see the shape of the roof as it is from the outside."

Most of the work has taken place in the last year, he added, after getting the relevant permissions.

He said the timing had been "just right" when it came on the market, and he had decided to put in an offer straight away.

After the property went to sealed bids, he said he asked the estate agent to include a personal note alongside his offer, which he believes persuaded the sellers to accept his bid.

"We didn't want to change the building in any way, we just wanted to restore it to the best it could be," he said.

"Once we got all the permissions in place it only took about nine months to go from probably a shell to the finished property."

He also said more people were now looking for staycations in the UK, and this had helped boost its appeal.

"It's the kind of place that me and my partner look for when we want to go away," he said.

"We don't tend to just find a house or a room or a hotel, we tend to look for something a bit more unusual."

Harrison said his first paying guest was a man from Stoke-on-Trent whose partner lived near Stafford when she was younger, and it was booked as a surprise for her birthday.

He added that a lot of the fixtures and fittings had been made bespoke for the property, and that giving it a new lease of life had provided him with a lot of satisfaction.

articles.title: In 2023, a California materials scientist built a device that pulled drinking water from desert air; it produced 35 litres a day at just 20% humidity
articles.summary: US News: In a groundbreaking development, a California materials scientist created a solar-powered device that extracts drinking water from arid desert air, producing 35 litres a day even at low humidity levels. This revolutionary technology promises to combat water scarcity in dry regions.
articles.body: In the summer of 2023, scientists from UC Berkeley took a machine that could be held by two hands to Death Valley National Park in North America, which is one of the most arid and hot locations on the continent and allowed it to operate using only the energy of the sun. It pulled water vapor out of the desert air, converted it to liquid and produced drinkable water without a battery, a plug, or any moving parts drawing outside power. The chemist behind the work, Omar Yaghi, had spent years building toward that single field test.The harvester ran on ambient sunlight aloneThis device uses a MOF, or metal-organic framework, an ultra-porous crystalline structure that Yaghi's team has studied for years. The specific MOF used here is MOF-303, an aluminum MOF that captures water molecules from the air at night, when humidity is usually higher in the desert and releases them during the day as sunlight warms the material. The resulting vapor condenses on a cooler surface within the device and flows into a container.How the output shifted with humidity Testing the same device in two very different climates allowed the team to isolate the effect of humidity. In Death Valley, the harvester achieved up to 210 grams of water per kilogram of MOF-303 per day in a single day-and-night cycle, marking the highest output the team recorded at that site. By comparison, in the milder, more humid air of Berkeley, the same device reached up to 285 grams per kilogram per day under similar passive operation, though Berkeley's daily averages ran lower on some days. The results appear in a 2023 paper in Nature Water, MOF water harvester produces water from Death Valley desert air in ambient sunlight, by Woochul Song, Zhiling Zheng, Ali Alawadhi and Yaghi, and they mark roughly double what an earlier passive version of the harvester had managed.An earlier MOF proved the concept could work at 20 percent humidityDeath Valley’s new technology is a further development of the tests done on the material by Yaghi and his team six years back, in collaboration with mechanical engineers from MIT. This project, which was done in 2017, involved a totally new material made up of zirconium and referred to as MOF-801. The results proved that even at low humidity levels between 20% and 30%, a solar-driven water harvester could generate significant quantities of water.The findings, published in Science as Water harvesting from air with metal-organic frameworks powered by natural sunlight, reported a yield of about 2.8 liters of water per kilogram of MOF per day at relative humidity as low as 20 percent, using only sunlight to drive the release step; some press accounts described the same result as roughly 2.8 liters over a 12-hour test window, though the paper itself reports it as a daily figure. The 2023 Nature Water study notes that switching from zirconium-based MOF-801, priced at $160 per kilogram, to aluminum-based MOF-303, priced at $3 per kilogram, made the harvester far cheaper to build; the higher water yield came from MOF-303's own adsorption behavior, not from its lower price.Why dry air poses the harder engineering challenge Water extraction from moist air is fairly easy since most dehumidifiers function on the principle of cooling air below its dew point. Nevertheless, air in the desert presents a different challenge. This is because at relative humidity less than 20%, the dew point may be below the freezing point, meaning that a lot of energy will be required for the process of condensation. MOFs are designed such that their pores are capable of adsorbing water molecules, even at very low levels of humidity, while heat can desorb them.From a two-hand prototype toward household-scale unitsThe Death Valley test was, by design, a proof‑of‑concept prototype rather than a final, household‑scale product. The scientists pointed out that the tiny size and limited daily amount of water provided by the device were more appropriate for proving the concept behind the chemical reaction rather than for providing enough drinking water for a family's daily needs. Yaghi also disclosed in a public interview that further development along the same lines of MOF chemistry greatly enhanced production, and his firm began manufacturing more efficient devices capable of producing water in quantities of dozens or even hundreds of liters each day.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ​In 2002, a collector bought a 75-cent record at a New York flea market; it turned out to be one of only two surviving Velvet Underground acetates and sold for $25,200
articles.summary: US News: During a stroll through the Chelsea fire sales, a collector got his hands on something one can only dream about. And yet, that was exactly what happen.
articles.body: During a stroll through the Chelsea fire sales, a collector got his hands on something one can only dream about. And yet, that was exactly what happened to Warren Hill in 2002. He picked up an acetate record at a flea market in New York for the price of a coffee. He bought one of only two surviving copies of The Velvet Underground's secret tape session. He eventually sold it for $25,200!He didn’t have a collector’s savvy eye. It was rather plain luck that landed him a piece of music history. When he bought the record alongside damaged LPs from estate sales and fire-damaged lots, he didn’t expect he was going to make a fortune out of it. He had no idea that the 1966 recording, known as the ‘Scepter Studios’ acetate, contained nine early versions of songs that would later appear on The Velvet Underground & Nico, the band’s influential 1967 debut album. Four years after finding it, Hill sold the acetate for $25,200, Rolling Stone reported.A rare recording on acetateThe acetate was created in April 1966, before The Velvet Underground had signed with a record label. Andy Warhol had already established himself as the band's manager. He knew The Velvet Underground's music was unlikely to appeal to major labels, so he planned a secret recording session.Engineer Norman Dolph recorded the band at Scepter Studios after hours. He was reportedly paid with a painting from Warhol for making the recording. Warhol took the acetate directly to the gatekeepers. Columbia said no. Atlantic said no. Elektra politely declined. It took Verve Records to finally agree to distribute the band's debut, which hit shelves in 1967 under the iconic banana sticker design.The Scepter recording remained buried, known only to those who had handled it in person. Warhol wanted to make the recording before the band signed to a label so record companies could not interfere with its music. After recording, Dolph sent the acetate to Columbia Records, Atlantic and Elektra. All of them said no. Verve Records eventually agreed to distribute the band's debut album. So, for years, the Scepter recording remained buried, and nobody knew about it other than the team. Only two original copies of the acetate are known to survive. The other is owned by Velvet Underground drummer Maureen Tucker.These acetates mean a lot in the music industry, though longevity is not their strongest suit. The material is unstable, so most collectors know that twenty to thirty spins can destroy the record. But, to everyone’s surprise, this particular disc somehow survived fire damage, decades of storage and the general degradation that time inflicts.Finding it in a flea marketIn 2002, record collector Warren Hill came across it at a street sale in New York City. The acetate record only cost him 75 cents. Four years later, he listed it on eBay and watched the bidding price climb past $150,000. But then the buyer backed out. He put the acetate up for auction again, this time with stricter requirements for potential buyers. The sale eventually settled at $25,200 with legitimate verification.The anonymous collector who bought it then chose a path most wouldn't. He locked the acetate away and never played it. Not once. He knew how fragile the record was. He wasn’t ready to take any risks. “It wasn’t worth it to me to even handle the record, let alone drag a needle across it. This is not a conventional record that can be played thousands and thousands of times. It’s an acetate; it’s the equivalent of a CD you’d burn 10 years ago,” he told Rolling Stone. He treated it as a financial stake in music history. And he was indeed right to.In 2012, when the 45th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition of The Velvet Underground & Nico arrived, it included a remastered version of these sessions on the fourth disc, pulled from Maureen Tucker's identical copy, the only other acetate known to exist. Record stores sold 5,000 limited copies during Record Store Day. Suddenly, millions could hear what Warhol had hidden. And the other copy was auctioned again, this time for even more.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Why Bangladesh has lost 1,000 lives to measles despite record vaccine drive
articles.summary: The nation has administered 20mn vaccines since April, but past slipups have led to a mounting death toll, say analysts
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – One-year-old Saif Hasan died within minutes of being taken into intensive care at Dhaka’s Infectious Diseases Hospital (IDH) on August 27.

The child from the southern Bangladesh district of Shariatpur had developed a fever and rashes days after receiving his first measles-rubella vaccine. His family wondered whether the vaccine had made him ill.

But Saif, who had been receiving treatment for a pre-existing respiratory illness, was likely infected with measles before the vaccine had time to protect him, Shrebash Paul, a junior consultant at the hospital, said. “The infection then aggravated his underlying condition.”

Saif’s death points to the challenge Bangladesh faces in containing a measles epidemic that is now believed to have killed more than 1,000 people since March 15 this year. Last year, Bangladesh recorded 132 measles cases in total, with zero deaths.

The deaths come despite an emergency campaign that has administered nearly 20 million vaccine doses over this period.

By September 9, health authorities had recorded 1,009 deaths – 100 among laboratory-confirmed measles patients and 909 classified as suspected measles deaths. Yet the same official data shows 19.75 million children vaccinated since the emergency campaign began in April against the target of 18 million.

But public health experts say that apparently extraordinary figure helps expose one of the problems Bangladesh has faced in controlling the epidemic: On the one hand, the original estimate of the children needing vaccines was too low, while on the other, national coverage figures can obscure pockets where large numbers of susceptible children remain.

A target that underestimated the problem

Bangladesh’s vulnerability to measles did not emerge overnight.

The South Asian nation of about 178 million people had been moving towards eliminating the disease before years of declining immunisation coverage left a growing number of children susceptible.

Bangladesh’s 2023 Coverage Evaluation Survey found that first-dose measles-rubella coverage had declined from 88.6 percent in 2019 to 86 percent in 2023, while second-dose coverage fell from 89 percent to 80.7 percent.

Routine immunisation was disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, while UNICEF has also cited misinformation and vaccine hesitancy among factors contributing to children missing vaccinations.

Besides, before this year’s effort, Bangladesh had not conducted a nationwide supplementary measles-rubella campaign since the last one ran from December 2020 to January 2021. Coverage therefore remained below the approximately 95 percent level needed to interrupt measles transmission, allowing the number of susceptible children to grow over successive years.

The problem worsened amid political upheaval following the July 2024 uprising, when then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was ousted, and disruptions to the country’s immunisation programme.

The change in government led to delays in vaccine procurement, said Mushtuq Hussain, a former principal scientific officer at Bangladesh’s Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). That, in turn, led to vaccine shortages in 2024 and 2025.

Cases began rising markedly in January 2026 and surged through March, prompting Bangladesh to notify the World Health Organization (WHO) of a nationwide outbreak on April 4. By mid-April, cases had been reported in 58 of the country’s 64 districts.

When the current outbreak accelerated, authorities launched emergency vaccination in high-risk areas on April 5, followed by a nationwide campaign later that month. Authorities set a target of about 18 million children aged six months to under five years when the measles-rubella vaccination campaign was launched on April 20.

Yet, about two months later, on June 28, the government’s campaign to administer Vitamin A supplements targeted about 24 million children in the same age group – a difference of nearly six million. That discrepancy helps explain how Bangladesh can now report vaccinating almost 20 million children – exceeding its original target – while susceptible children continue to be found.

Hussain of the IEDCR questioned the population estimates used to set the vaccination target, saying they underestimated the number of eligible children.

Nationwide averages can also mask local gaps. “You have to maintain equity,” Hussain said, arguing that at least 95 percent coverage must be achieved across communities, including among hard-to-reach and mobile populations.

Measles is among the world’s most contagious diseases, meaning even relatively small concentrations of unprotected people can sustain transmission.

Hussain said high national average coverage rates could conceal immunity gaps in individual communities, allowing the virus to continue circulating.

A second epidemiologist with extensive experience in Bangladesh’s immunisation programme, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, said authorities needed to analyse cases by age, vaccination history and location and use the findings to identify susceptible populations.

Without targeted vaccination of those populations, the epidemiologist said, transmission was likely to continue even if overall case numbers declined. Doctors treating patients are seeing evidence of those gaps.

Paul, the doctor at the IDH in Dhaka, told Al Jazeera that the majority of measles patients currently being admitted were unvaccinated. Some of the children now being treated had missed the vaccination campaign because they had been ill at the time.

Hospital admissions have nevertheless declined from their peak, Paul said, suggesting the vaccination programme has had a substantial effect. Still, children continue to arrive.

The IDH’s mortality review provides another clue to why the outbreak has been so deadly.

As of August 23, the hospital had recorded 3,167 suspected measles cases, 537 laboratory-confirmed cases, and 57 confirmed or suspected measles deaths this year.

The deaths were overwhelmingly concentrated among very young children. Of the 57 who died, 49 – about 86 percent – were younger than 15 months, while 31 were younger than nine months, the age at which children in Bangladesh routinely receive their first measles-rubella dose.

Forty-seven of the 57 people who died – 83 percent – had received no measles vaccine, according to the hospital’s analysis. Pneumonia was recorded in 50 of the documented deaths – making it the leading responsible complication.

Paul said doctors were particularly concerned about infections among infants who had not yet reached the age for routine vaccination.

The IDH is studying children infected before nine months of age and their mothers to better understand the factors behind those infections. The hospital data should not be read as nationally representative, Paul said, adding that the IDH is a specialist referral hospital that receives serious patients from Dhaka and other parts of Bangladesh.

But the numbers provide a window into the children at greatest risk once measles spreads widely.

Health officials, meanwhile, say reported case numbers may not fully reflect the underlying trend.

Halimur Rashid, director of disease control at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) — the government agency responsible for overseeing public health programmes — said authorities were preparing a further round of vaccinations, expected to begin within the next two weeks.

The next challenge will be reaching children missed by previous rounds. Experts say success will depend less on another large national coverage figure than on micro-planning – identifying susceptible children community by community and ensuring vaccinators reach them.

Hussain said authorities should consider extending vaccination to older children where surveillance identifies significant immunity gaps.

The epidemiologist who requested anonymity said vaccination may need to reach children up to 15 years old in affected areas.

But for too many families in Bangladesh, it is already too late.

Among those who fell through those gaps was Mostakim, a nine-month-old from east-central Kishoreganj district. He had not been vaccinated against measles.

articles.title: A couple spent five years searching Google Maps for an island; they found a 5-acre Finnish island and built their solar-powered dream home
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Finnish couple spent five years searching Google Maps and government property records for an island they could call their own before discovering a 5.
articles.body: A Finnish couple spent five years searching Google Maps and government property records for an island they could call their own before discovering a 5-acre patch of land in the country’s vast archipelago. Aleksi Hautamäki and Milla Selkimäki had explored the region for years and wanted a secluded place that was remote enough to feel like an escape but still suitable for building a home. In 2018, they finally found the uninhabited island, then sold their Helsinki apartment to help fund the purchase and construction. They transformed the rocky landscape into Project Ö, a compact retreat made up of two buildings that together cover about 70 square metres. The home runs off-grid using solar power and filtered seawater, while its design takes cues from traditional Finnish cabins and Japanese minimalism.How the couple found their island after five years of searching Google MapsAleksi had been familiar with the Finnish Archipelago since childhood, having spent summers exploring it with his father, while Milla had also spent time in the region. After they met, the couple began spending their summers boating through the archipelago and around 2015 started considering the idea of owning an island. With suitable properties rarely appearing on the conventional market, they began searching for apparently empty islands using maps. They would identify potential sites, check local ownership records and contact the owners to ask whether they would consider selling. The process was painstaking and continued for five years before they discovered Skjulskäret, a roughly two-hectare island on the edge of the Archipelago National Park.The 5-acre island became their blank canvasThe island was completely uninhabited when the couple acquired it and offered a mixture of rocky bays, pine woodland and sheltered areas along the shoreline. One bay was deep enough to serve as a natural dock, while another provided a suitable swimming spot. Its relatively small size was also part of the attraction, as Aleksi did not want a huge island with large areas that would remain unused. The couple completed the purchase in 2018 and began developing the property around the existing landscape rather than trying to turn it into a conventional suburban-style home.They designed a compact island retreatThe couple's professional backgrounds shaped the project from the beginning. Aleksi is a spatial designer, while Milla works as a creative director, allowing them to approach the property as both a home and a design project. Their plan was to fit everything they needed into as little space as possible. The main cabin contains living, cooking and sleeping areas along with a bathroom and sauna, while a second building serves as a workshop and additional functional space. Together, the two buildings cover about 70 square metres, yet the layout was designed to accommodate up to 10 adults when required.The architecture follows the rocky landscapeRather than imposing a large structure on the island, the couple designed narrow buildings inspired by traditional Finnish archipelago architecture. Gabled roofs, long eaves and vertical timber cladding give the cabins a distinctly Nordic appearance, while large windows provide changing views of the sea and surrounding landscape. Aleksi also drew inspiration from Japanese small-house design, particularly its emphasis on making compact spaces functional without filling them with unnecessary features. The buildings were positioned to work with the island's natural contours, creating a retreat that feels closely connected to the surrounding rocks, trees and water.The home operates without mainland utilitiesProject Ö was designed as a self-sufficient, off-grid retreat. Solar panels supply the island's electricity, while seawater is filtered to provide drinking water. A seawater reverse-osmosis system was chosen instead of drilling a conventional well, with the purification system powered using solar energy. The buildings also have running water, a flush toilet, heating, cooling and a modern kitchen. Hot water and underfloor heating are supported by the sauna stove, allowing the compact retreat to function despite its remote location.The couple built around the island's limitationsLiving on a remote island meant the design had to account for everything that could not simply be connected to a mainland network. The couple considered factors such as the direction of sunlight and prevailing winds when planning the buildings and outdoor areas. Aleksi also designed and partly built parts of the project himself, including the jetty and wooden walkways that connect different areas of the island. The result was not simply a house placed on an island but a network of compact spaces designed around the site's natural characteristics and the practical realities of island living.Project Ö eventually opened to guestsWhat began as the couple's private retreat eventually became a holiday destination. After the project attracted attention through social media and international architecture and travel coverage, they began sharing the island with visitors. Project Ö's current website describes the original island as Skärö and offers stays with boat transfers, a private beach, sauna, hot tub, kitchen and other facilities. The property is now one of three islands operated under the Project Ö name, extending the couple's original idea into a wider island hospitality venture.The island remains at the heart of the projectToday, the original retreat combines the solitude that attracted the couple with the comforts they deliberately designed into the property. Guests can reach the island by travelling from Helsinki towards the archipelago before taking a boat across the surrounding waters. Once there, the experience centres on the landscape itself, with rocky shores, pine forest, swimming areas, outdoor dining spaces and a wood-heated sauna overlooking the sea. What began with years of searching for a small piece of Finland's archipelago has evolved into a private island retreat built around compact design, renewable energy and life largely independent of mainland infrastructure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
