articles.title: Scientists used a microlight aircraft to teach bald ibises a migration route; years later, Europe got its first self-sustaining colony in 400 years
articles.summary: Europe News: For centuries, the northern bald ibis was missing from Europe's skies, its migratory population wiped out in Central Europe by the 17th century. Bring.
articles.body: For centuries, the northern bald ibis was missing from Europe's skies, its migratory population wiped out in Central Europe by the 17th century. Bringing it back required more than releasing captive-bred birds into the Alps: conservationists first had to teach them where to go. The Waldrappteam found an ingenious solution, training young ibises to follow a microlight aircraft south towards their wintering grounds in Italy. The experiment began producing remarkable results. In 2007, the birds completed their first successful flight over the Alps behind the aircraft, and by 2011 they were returning without human guidance. Years later, Europe had its first self-sustaining colony in 400 years.Microlight aircraft helped bald ibises relearn their ancient migration routeAccording to the study published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘On the road to self-sustainability: reintroduced migratory European northern bald ibises Geronticus eremita still need management interventions for population viability’, the northern bald ibis, Geronticus eremita, was once a familiar sight in Central Europe, particularly around the Alps. The birds survived in the region until the 17th century, when intensive hunting drove them to extinction. Chicks were considered a delicacy, and pressure from hunting eventually wiped the species out in Central Europe. The zoo describes the Waldrappteam as an effort to restore the migratory bird to the Alps after centuries of absence.The disappearance was particularly difficult to reverse because migration is not simply an instinct that every young bird can perform without guidance. The Oryx study explains that juveniles normally learn their migration route by following other members of their species to the wintering grounds. That created a problem for captive-bred birds being prepared for release: without experienced migrants to follow, simply putting them back into the landscape would not necessarily give them the knowledge needed to complete their annual journey.Human foster parents trained young ibises to follow a microlightAccording to Hellabrunn Zoo, the Waldrappteam developed a human-led migration system to solve that problem. Zoo-hatched chicks had human foster parents, and once the young birds could fly, they were trained to follow a microlight aircraft. In autumn, the aircraft travelled south towards the birds' wintering grounds, with the young ibises following behind. Hellabrunn explains that the birds would then return to their breeding grounds using the route they had learned.Birds in the research either had been raised in zoo breeding colonies and prepared for release by human foster parents, or had been born in the wild to previously released birds. The researchers state that birds prepared for release were “trained to follow a microlight plane” to the common wintering ground, where they were integrated into the population. From 2011 onwards, increasing numbers of chicks were instead raised naturally by their biological parents and could follow other ibises on their first migration.The first successful microlight migration came in 2007The first breakthrough came in 2007, when the Waldrappteam successfully flew northern bald ibises over the Alps to Italy behind a microlight aircraft. Four years later, in 2011, the birds began returning to their starting point in Burghausen, Germany, without being led. The project then took several more years to establish a self-sufficient breeding colony, becoming the zoo's first such colony in Europe for 400 years.The wider project grew steadily. The scientific paper says that a European research project began in 2002 and became a European Union LIFE+ funded translocation and conservation project in 2014. By late 2021, the reintroduced Waldrappteam population contained about 200 birds across four breeding colonies: two in southern Germany and two in Austria. The colonies were treated as one population because the birds shared the same wintering ground at WWF Oasi Laguna di Orbetello in Tuscany, Italy.Illegal hunting and power poles remained major threatsResearchers analysed 384 northern bald ibises from generations produced between 2008 and 2019, finding survival probabilities of 0.64–0.78, with 45% of mature females reproducing and an average of 2.15 fledglings per nest. However, their population viability analysis estimated a growth rate of 0.95 and a 24% extinction probability within 50 years. Of 326 management scenarios tested, 94% met the study's criteria for a viable population, showing that further action was still needed. The main threats were illegal hunting in Italy and electrocution on unsecured power poles, while retrofitting dangerous poles in Germany reduced the country's electrocution loss rate by 91%.By teaching captive-bred ibises to follow a microlight aircraft, conservationists recreated the migration knowledge that had disappeared with the original population. The birds eventually learned to make the journey without human guidance, while later generations could learn the route naturally from other ibises.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hong Kong’s $28.6bn project: Villages make way for new homes, logistics hubs and tech city
articles.summary: News News: Hong Kong has begun clearing land for a massive Northern Metropolis development that will transform villages, farmland and wetlands into housing, logi.
articles.body: Hong Kong has begun clearing land for a massive Northern Metropolis development that will transform villages, farmland and wetlands into housing, logistics and high-tech projects, with the government estimating the project will cost at least HK$224 billion ($28.6 billion).The project has already entered a key phase. Last month, the first large-scale land sale in the Northern Metropolis was awarded to a consortium of six companies, including Chinese state-owned enterprises and e-commerce giant JD.com. The consortium plans to develop housing and a logistics centre in the area.The development is expected to eventually cover about 30,000 hectares (74,000 acres), roughly a third of Hong Kong. Authorities say it will accommodate around 2.5 million residents and create 650,000 jobs.For property developers, the project represents one of Hong Kong's biggest new land and infrastructure opportunities. For residents of the affected villages, it means losing homes and communities that have existed for generations.Chan Yuk-tong, 71, is among those being displaced. He had hoped to spend his remaining years in the small blue-brick houses where he was born and raised. His ancestral home is now due to be demolished."I can't bear to leave... If not for the government developing this area, I would likely spend the rest of my life here. After all, I belong here," Chan told AFP as he packed up belongings in his yard.Housing, logistics and a new economic centreThe Northern Metropolis was announced five years ago as a major urban expansion project. It is designed to create a new economic centre in Hong Kong's northern New Territories, close to the mainland Chinese border.The development will include residential areas, logistics facilities and high-tech clusters. It is also intended to strengthen Hong Kong's links with Macau and nine mainland Chinese cities that form the Greater Bay Area.The government has described the project as a "new economic engine". It expects the development to eventually contribute about 13% of Hong Kong's GDP, based on estimates cited from banks over a roughly 20-year period.The final bill, however, could be significantly higher. While the government estimates the cost at HK$224 billion, S&P has put the potential cost at more than HK$360 billion.That has raised questions over whether the expected economic and property gains will justify the scale of investment."Do we need to build it so big? Is it too ambitious?" said Brian Wong of Liber Research Community, an NGO focused on land issues.Land acquisition comes at a social costAt least 25 villages are expected to be demolished to make way for the project, according to Liber.Government departments told AFP they want to integrate rural areas into the wider development. But they said Chan's ancestral houses did not have enough cultural significance to warrant preservation.Niki So, 42, is another resident affected by the redevelopment. Her family had lived in the village for three generations. She received a public housing flat as compensation, but said she would miss a community where neighbours had become like family.In July, dozens of Lands Department officials and police entered her village and declared the area government property."I hope the development here will go well, that it will thrive," So said."If it doesn't turn out as expected then I think the sacrifice of this village would be quite unfortunate."Mainland companies seen as key to property demandThe Northern Metropolis is also being positioned as a bridge between Hong Kong's property market and the wider Greater Bay Area economy.Hannah Jeong of commercial real estate firm CBRE said mainland Chinese companies are likely to be among the first to take advantage of the government's support for the area. They could establish research centres and benefit from Hong Kong's tax regime, talent pool and access to data and capital."With that flow, more manpower coming in, talent coming in... forefign companies will also gradually (invest)," Jeong said.The strategy is aimed at building a high-tech ecosystem that can attract both Chinese and international businesses.Hong Kong, however, faces strong competition from established mainland technology centres such as Shenzhen and Hangzhou."Less relevant for China's national tech ambitions" than mainland powerhouses like Shenzhen, said Gary Ng, a senior economist at Natixis.Hong Kong's advantage, he said, lies in areas such as international connectivity, university research and its deep capital markets.Cross-border links key to successThe success of the property-led expansion will depend heavily on how easily people, businesses and capital can move between Hong Kong and mainland China."The biggest hurdle to the Northern Metropolis' success is how to maintain an efficient cross-border flow, and at the same time maintaining the confidence that the international community has in Hong Kong's uniqueness", said Wilson Chan, co-founder of the Pagoda Institute think tank.The project is part of a broader push to integrate Hong Kong more closely with mainland China. That process has accelerated since Beijing imposed a national security law on the city in 2020 following large pro-democracy protests.Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute, said the changes had reduced opposition to deeper integration.It "effectively put an end to the 'one country, two systems' framework that allowed Hong Kong a 'high degree of autonomy', so greater integration with the Greater Bay Area would logically follow," he told AFP.For Hong Kong, the Northern Metropolis now represents both a huge real estate expansion and a long-term bet on a new economic corridor. For the communities being cleared to make way for it, the transformation has already begun.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd jailed for attacking his partner
articles.summary: Jack Shepherd was sentenced at Isleworth Crown Court after previously admitting the violent assault.
articles.body:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

Mitigating, George Payne said Shepherd, who attended by videolink from HMP Swaleside in Kent, was "genuinely very ashamed of his behaviour".

"The behaviour is driven by his abuse of alcohol and is a feature that has existed for a long time," Payne said.

Judge Martin Edmunds rejected that, and said he had "no faith" in Shepherd's remorse, adding: "Your pattern is to commit offences and afterwards apologise, and produce excuses. Your prepared statement sought to shift blame anywhere but yourself."

Speedboat killer admits violent attack on woman

Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd returned to jail

Speedboat killer jailed after fleeing UK

Judge Edmunds previously told the court the law did not allow him to add any more time to the term Shepherd was already serving, and his most recent sentence would be served concurrently to his current sentence.

He is due to be released in January 2029.

Following Brown's death, Shepherd went on the run in Georgia. He was convicted in his absence of manslaughter by gross negligence following an Old Bailey trial, and was eventually extradited back to the UK to serve his sentence.

Brown, from Clacton, Essex, was fatally thrown from his speedboat boat on the River Thames, when it hit a submerged tree trunk, in December 2015.

Shepherd was pulled out of the Thames alive, but Brown was found unconscious and unresponsive and died later in hospital.

articles.title: In 1985, Canadian athlete Rick Hansen began a 40,075-km wheelchair journey through 34 countries that raised $26 million; 40 years later, his foundation is renewing the push for a world without barriers
articles.summary: Rest of World News: What began as one man pushing his wheelchair across the world became a movement that continues four decades later. On March 21, 1985, Canadian athlete.
articles.body: What began as one man pushing his wheelchair across the world became a movement that continues four decades later. On March 21, 1985, Canadian athlete Rick Hansen set out from Vancouver on what would become the Man In Motion World Tour, a 26-month journey through 34 countries and across more than 40,000 kilometres. According to the Rick Hansen Foundation, Hansen and his team ultimately covered 40,075 kilometres and raised $26 million, while drawing global attention to the potential of people with disabilities. In 2026, the foundation is marking the tour’s 40th-anniversary legacy by renewing its call for a world without barriers.The journey that started a movementHansen was already an accomplished wheelchair athlete when he began planning the journey. His goal was not simply to complete an extraordinary physical challenge. He wanted to change how society viewed people with disabilities and demonstrate what could be achieved when barriers were removed. The tour began in Vancouver on March 21, 1985. Hansen and his team travelled through 34 countries across four continents, eventually returning to Vancouver on May 22, 1987. The official Rick Hansen Foundation account records the total distance as 40,075 kilometres, roughly the circumference of the Earth. Hansen averaged about 85 kilometres a day and spent an average of eight hours a day wheeling.The journey was physically demanding, involving long stretches of road, difficult terrain and changing weather conditions. But the larger challenge was social. Hansen wanted the tour to draw attention to the abilities and potential of people with disabilities while highlighting the physical and attitudinal barriers that prevented many from participating fully in everyday life.$26 million raised and a lasting legacyWhen Hansen completed the tour in 1987, it had become much more than an athletic achievement. The journey raised $26 million and helped generate widespread discussion about disability, accessibility and inclusion. The foundation says the tour helped change perceptions of people with disabilities and contributed to a broader public conversation around making communities more accessible. The legacy continued after Hansen returned home. In 1988, the organisation that grew out of the Man In Motion movement was established and later became the Rick Hansen Foundation. Its work expanded beyond awareness campaigns to include accessibility initiatives, leadership programmes, scholarships and support for spinal cord injury research and care.The foundation's focus today is built around a broader understanding of accessibility. Physical barriers remain an important concern, but the organisation also identifies attitudinal barriers and outdated systems, laws and policies as obstacles that can prevent people with disabilities from participating fully in society.From one journey to a wider accessibility movementFour decades after Hansen first set out, the central idea behind the journey remains relevant. According to the Rick Hansen Foundation, people with disabilities continue to encounter barriers in places where they live, work, learn and play. Its current work includes an Accessibility Certification programme designed to help businesses and communities improve the meaningful accessibility of the built environment. The foundation also runs programmes aimed at young people, supports leadership and scholarships, and has expanded its work into areas such as outdoor accessibility.The 40th-anniversary campaign, a continuation of the movement sparked by the Man In Motion World Tour, is built around the idea that accessibility is an ongoing effort rather than a problem that can be solved through a single achievement. The organisation is encouraging supporters to help remove barriers and create spaces where people of all abilities can participate fully. The anniversary also offers a chance to look back at how far the movement has come. Hansen's journey helped put disability inclusion into a much wider public conversation, while the foundation has spent the years since working to turn that awareness into practical changes.The journey is still in motionThe significance of the Man In Motion World Tour lies not only in the distance Hansen travelled, but in what the journey represented. He set out in 1985 with the belief that barriers could be challenged by showing the world what people with disabilities could accomplish. More than 40 years later, that message remains at the centre of the foundation's work.The original tour eventually ended in Vancouver, but its larger journey did not. From accessibility in buildings and public spaces to changing attitudes and creating more inclusive communities, the push for a world without barriers continues. Hansen's 40,075-kilometre journey therefore remains more than a remarkable chapter in sporting history; it became the starting point for a movement that is still working to make inclusion part of everyday life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Europe Gas Prices Jump 6% as Saudi Pipeline Shutdown Rattles Markets
articles.summary: European gas prices jumped 6% Monday to $97.31/MWh after Saudi Arabia shut a key pipeline, as Middle East tensions squeeze global LNG supply.
articles.body:
Europe's benchmark natural gas prices jumped by 6% at Monday market opening in Amsterdam as oil prices rallied amid the escalation in the Middle East that threatens the recovery of energy flows.

The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, soared by 6% as of 7:50 a.m. Amsterdam time on Monday, to hit the highest level since the 2022-2023 crisis.

At $97.31 (84.275 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh), the price now exceeds the January 2023 levels, when Europe faced the first winter without most of the Russian pipeline gas supply.

Gas prices in Europe, fresh off five consecutive weeks of weekly gains, continued their rally on Monday, as risks to supply of oil and gas in the Middle East materially increased over the weekend after Saudi Arabia shut down its key East-West oil pipeline that helps it bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

European gas prices have rallied in recent weeks as gas storage sites across Europe are less than 70% full compared to 82% for this time of year in 2025 and a five-year average of above 80%.

Europe is heading into winter with one of the lowest levels of gas in storage in the past two decades as the war in the Middle East crippled LNG supply from Qatar, sent gas and LNG prices in Europe and Asia skyrocketing, and intensified competition for readily available global LNG cargoes that don't need to cross geopolitically charged chokepoints.

"The potential for a global 'fight for fuel' is there, particularly in a colder winter," Go Katayama, principal insight analyst for LNG at intelligence firm Kpler, told Bloomberg earlier this month.

In a sign of intensifying competition, Asia's spot LNG price surged last week to the highest level since 2022 .

"The disruption has forced buyers in Europe and Asia to compete more aggressively for alternative cargoes and has helped push European natural gas above USD 140 per barrel equivalent," Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, said last week.

articles.title: Anthrax outbreak: Zambians warned not to eat dead wildlife
articles.summary: At least 12 people are being treated for anthrax after eating infected meat from wildlife carcasses.
articles.body:
Authorities in Zambia have warned people not to eat meat from wildlife after dozens of wild animals, including hippos, elephants, buffalo and a crocodile died following an anthrax outbreak.

A disaster management agency official said over the weekend that 12 people had been infected with the disease after consuming dead wildlife in the Munyamadzi River area.

The official urged the public not to consume meat from animals that die naturally or from unknown causes, while urging the public to report any such cases.

Authorities have also called for hunting in the affected area to be suspended until the extent of the disease and associated risks are established.

Officials have not yet ascertained the full geographical extent of the latest outbreak, with surveillance and laboratory investigations ongoing.

Anthrax is endemic to Zambia but human deaths are not common. In 2023, the country experienced what was described as an "unprecedented outbreak", which killed four people and spread to nine out of 10 provinces.

Another large-scale outbreak was reported in 2011, with more than 500 cases, when five people died after consuming meat from infected hippos.

In the latest outbreak in the Munyamadzi Game Management Area, in Muchinga province, Zambia's Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit said 46 hippos, eight elephants, five buffaloes and one crocodile had died since July.

"The sad story about the deaths of this wildlife is that the carcasses ended up being eaten by the local people - that's what they depend on for their food," said the unit's national coordinator Norman Chipakupaku.

No human deaths have been reported, and the 12 infected people are currently receiving treatment.

Anthrax is caused by a bacteria called Bacillus anthracis, which largely survives as spores that hide away in soil for years before entering an animal through inhalation or a cut or wound.

It mainly affects grazing animals and can lead to sudden death. It can be transmitted from animals to humans through contact with contaminated animal products.

Zambians have been urged not to consume, sell, distribute or handle meat from animals that have died suddenly or from suspected anthrax. The public has also been advised against handling wild animals.

articles.title: Shot down in Iran, hunted for 50 hours: New details emerge on US rescue op for Air Force officers Alpha, Bravo
articles.summary: US News: NEW DELHI: A newly declassified video has revealed details of a high-risk US military operation to rescue an Air Force officer who spent nearly 50 hou.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A newly declassified video has revealed details of a high-risk US military operation to rescue an Air Force officer who spent nearly 50 hours wounded and hiding behind enemy lines in Iran after his F-15E fighter jet was shot down in April.More than 90 US service members were deployed on the ground during the rescue operation, while hundreds of personnel were involved in the air and several thousand others provided support, according to CBS News' '60 Minutes'.The operation involved combat search-and-rescue teams, CIA intelligence and deception efforts, helicopters, bombers and drones, as US forces raced against time to locate and extract the officer, identified by his callsign "Bravo".Bravo was the weapons-systems officer aboard the two-seat F-15E, operating under the mission callsign Dude 44. The aircraft was hit by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile during a strike mission near Isfahan on April 2.The missile damaged Bravo's parachute and he fell at an estimated 70 to 100 mph before hitting the ground in a mountainous desert region. He suffered a broken back, arm and shoulder and landed around five miles from his pilot, "Alpha"."At one point when I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I've ever seen," Bravo said in his first public account of the incident."So I paused, right then, and I prayed, 'Lord, your will be done. But if I'm getting through this, I need help.'"First rescue succeeds, Bravo remains missingAlpha ejected safely and was rescued during a risky daytime operation about six hours after the aircraft was shot down. US helicopters involved in the mission came under fire as they entered and exited the area."It was a gun fight all the way in and all the way out," US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said. "But they got Alpha back."However, the rescue team could not locate Bravo and had to withdraw, leaving the injured officer alone behind enemy lines.Bravo, despite his injuries, moved away from his landing site and climbed towards a 7,000-foot ridgeline, where he found a position from which he could remain concealed."Never let a lack of motivation put you on Iranian TV," Bravo said.As Iranian forces searched for the downed crew, US officials tracked their movements. Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Iranian ground forces came within a few hundred metres of Bravo."There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Caine said.Bravo eventually managed to contact US forces and informed them that he was injured but still moving. However, a planned rescue could not immediately be carried out."That was a really tough decision," Hegseth said. "I'll never forget, you know, being in the situation room and saying, 'OK, I guess we're gonna roll 24,' which means, 'Hey, Bravo's going to be out there for basically 24 hours more.'"CIA deception, air strikes clear rescue pathBravo survived another full day in the cold and windy high-desert terrain with almost no food or water.The CIA played a key role in the search, using intelligence capabilities and a multi-pronged deception campaign to confuse Iranian forces trying to locate him. The agency also used technology to pinpoint his position.US bombers and drones then struck Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces in the area where Bravo was hiding, helping clear the way for the second rescue attempt.The rescue force included more than 90 US service members on the ground, marking the first deployment of US troops on Iranian soil in 46 years, according to Adm. Brad Cooper, the US Central Command commander.Several hundred personnel were involved in the air operation, while thousands more supported the mission from elsewhere."I think what you need to know is we would have sent more to go get the back-seater," Caine said, referring to Bravo's position in the fighter jet.‘Let's go’: Final extractionThe rescue force arrived aboard two large search-and-rescue aircraft, which landed on a makeshift desert airstrip. Small "Little Bird" helicopters were then used to reach Bravo on the distant ridgeline.After spending nearly two days wounded and isolated behind enemy lines, Bravo finally saw the rescuers approaching.He described the moment as "one of the greatest moments of my life".When his rescuers reached him, Bravo said, he had only one thing to say:"Let's go."The mission, however, was not yet over.The rescue aircraft became stuck in the desert sand and their landing gear could not be freed. More than 90 elite US service members were left stranded on the ground until a clandestine Air Force unit arrived to assist them.The US military ultimately destroyed the two stranded aircraft, each worth about $100 million, along with the Little Bird helicopters to prevent sensitive technology from falling into Iranian hands.Fifty hours after being shot down, Bravo was finally brought to safety as the sun rose on Easter Sunday.Reflecting on the mission, Bravo said the operation represented more than his own survival."It's a story of the teamwork, the training, of the faith, of the decisions and the leadership to do something that will live in history as an example of what America's willing to do, in order to uphold our promise and leave no man behind."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: John Swinney aiming for independence referendum by 2031
articles.summary: The FM has signed an agreement with other nationalist leaders predicting "Westminster's time is coming to an end".
articles.body:
First Minister John Swinney says he wants to hold a second Scottish independence referendum by 2031.

The SNP leader also predicted that Andy Burnham would be the last prime minister of the UK following talks with nationalist leaders in Cardiff.

Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald and Sinn Feinn vice-president Michelle O'Neill have signed a joint declaration stating that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

Burnham's spokesman said the Labour leader was focused on easing the cost of living crisis rather than on "constitutional debates".

Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say

Photo call or 'pivotal moment' - How significant is leaders summit?

PM says second Scottish independence referendum remains 'off limits'

Following elections in Scotland and Wales in May, the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all represented by nationalist first ministers, although O'Neill represents one half of Stormont's power-sharing administration.

In the joint statement, ap Iorwerth, Swinney, O'Neill and McDonald said that "there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end".

Meeting in their capacities as party leaders, they stated: "Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people."

At a news conference, Swinney said he wanted to ensure Scots "have a choice on their constitutional future" in this Holyrood term, which is due to end in 2031.

He predicted that Burnham would be the last UK prime minister, adding: "The people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum, will take that choice, because all of the information that we see in front of us about the trends in opinion polling indicate that's the preference of the people of Scotland."

Constitutional change 'very much on the table'

Swinney claimed the "moment has now come" for a second referendum.

He noted that the Scottish Parliament has the largest number of pro-independence MSPs in its history - despite the SNP losing seats in May .

Together with the Scottish Greens there are a now total of 73 pro-independence MSPs, an increase of one, although their share of the vote fell to about 41%.

The first minister also cited the "mood of the Scottish people" as expressed in May and support for independence in opinion polls which in recent months have suggested a small majority in favour.

Swinney said the party leaders had agreed that there must be "no obstacles to the people of our countries expressing their right to self-determination".

"We will each individually be responsible for our own journeys but we are absolutely united by that principle of self-determination," Swinney told the conference.

Ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, called for a fundamental redesign of UK constitutional framework, envisioning independent nations working together. He added that the "current status quo is not tenable".

O'Neill, the Northern Irish first minister, said the party leaders agreed that "Westminster does not and will never serve our people well".

She insisted constitutional change was "very much on the table" despite Burnham's recent comments.

Swinney has said that a referendum could be held as soon as 2028 . However, questions remain about the mechanism through which that could be achieved.

Scotland voted in 2014 to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.

Pressure from the SNP for a second vote ramped up following the 2016 Brexit referendum, with Nicola Sturgeon arguing there had been a material change in circumstances.

However, successive prime ministers have refused to countenance another poll. And in 2022, the Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament could not hold another referendum without the consent of Westminster.

At Prime Minister's Questions last week, Burnham said there would not be a second referendum until there is "majority public support".

He reiterated the following day in a letter to Swinney that a referendum was "off limits".

The Labour leader said that the 2014 referendum was based on a shared agreement between the Scottish and UK governments that it was right to hold one, but that there was now no similar consensus.

He also highlighted Labour's manifesto commitment opposing independence and another referendum.

Responding to the Cardiff talks, Burnham's spokesman said he was "committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the union".

He added: "The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around our shared values and problem-solving, rather than division, and the prime minister will continue to ease pressures on household finances, and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums."

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said: "Many people across Scotland will recoil at the sight of John Swinney joining forces with Sinn Fein in their shared desire to destroy the United Kingdom.

"They will also be appalled by the SNP's continued disrespect towards the majority of Scots who reject separation and want the devolved government in Edinburgh to get on with its job."

Liberal Democrat MSP David Green said Swinney "should have used this summit to find common purpose in pushing power out to communities".

articles.title: £100,000 boost for West Midlands community eco-friendly projects
articles.summary: Community groups and young people across the West Midlands are being invited to apply for a grant.
articles.body:
A share of £100,000 is being offered to community groups and young people to be used for environmentally-friendly projects.

Groups can apply for up to £5,000 from the grant, which is being given out by the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) as part of its Circular Economy Call to Action Fund.

The authority has teamed up with Bloomberg Philanthropies to set up a separate pot for 15 to 24-year-olds, the Youth Climate Action Fund, which offers grants of up to £2,500.

"There are so many brilliant things happening in our communities to make them greener, healthier and more resilient," West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker said.

He added: "From planting trees and encouraging people to walk and cycle, to repairing rather than throwing things away.

"These may seem like small things but they are making a big difference to people's lives and helping to create a real sense of pride in these neighbourhoods.

"I'm all for that, so I'm getting behind these community groups with the funding and expertise they need to get more great ideas off the ground and widen their impact."

Projects need to have a focus on improving air quality, helping communities adapt to climate change or restoring nature across Wolverhampton, Sandwell, Walsall, Dudley, Birmingham, Solihull and Coventry.

articles.title: Opera singer leads Scottish takeover of Last Night of the Proms
articles.summary: Nicky Spence from Dumfries got the crowd laughing and cheering with a mash-up of traditional and modern music combined with dance moves and patriotic outfits.
articles.body:
When opera singer Nicky Spence took to the famous stage of London's Royal Albert Hall for the Last Night Proms, just a tartan scarf hinted at his roots.

But when he ripped off his "boring black trousers" to reveal a pair of tartan trews during a rendition of Donald, Where's Your Troosers? there was no doubt of his heritage.

It was part of Scotch Snap - a medley of traditional and modern classics - which the Dumfries native combined with dance moves and a series of patriotic outfits.

And it ensured the audience were treated to performances of The Proclaimers' I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles) and Bacara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie alongside the more traditional Rule Britannia! and Sit Down, Your're Rocking the Boat.

Spence, who now lives in Paisley with his husband and child, told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that the show was "such a blast".

"Everybody loved it, it was amazing - like a chip fire," he added.

"Like Bucks Fizz when there was lots of Velcro, I came on with some very boring black trousers and then whipped them off during Donald, Where's Your Troosers?

"I think that got everybody's pulses racing a la Magic Mike."

It was the world premiere of the medley, which was arranged by Stuart Calvert, and also featured traditional songs like The Bonnie Banks o' Loch Lomond.

Dance routines with two dancers dressed in red tartan kilts and bonnets accompanied the music.

But laughter came from the audience when Spence pulled off two costume changes.

He closed out his performance in a black T-shirt with gold sequined sleeves and a red pair of tartan trews, while a traditionally-dressed bagpiper accompanied the orchestra.

Spence said he spent a lot of time working with the arranger to choose the music, curate and trim the showcase.

"I put my finger up the zeitgeist to see what was hot at the time and I thought we have got to include Yes Sir, I Can Boogie," he said.

The Spanish duo Baccara's disco hit from 1977 became Scotland's unofficial national anthem ahead of Euro 2020.

The song travelled with the Tartan Army to the World Cup this summer, where it continued to be belted out by fans at home and at the tournament.

For Spence, however, the song did not even touch the sides of his vocal range, who is a specialist opera singer and has toured with Katherine Jenkins and Dame Shirley Bassey.

"Singing things like this is like sorbet compared to the rest of my life, which is like a heavy meal.

"Richard Wagner, Strauss and Mozart are beautiful but quite heavy weather stuff and much harder to sing than Yes Sir, I Can Boogie."

He added he was more concerned about the dancing than the singing during his performance.

Spence said it had been a long time since he had worn Scottish dress on stage but he had recently moved back to Scotland and was happy to be back.

"I had a record contract when I was about 21 years old with Universal Records and I was called The Scottish Tenor so I sang a lot of Robert Burns and wore a kilt most of the day," he said.

"Then I ditched it all and went into opera."

He joked if anyone wants to hear Yes Sir, I Can Boogie, he will sing it again.

The tenor also portrayed the prince from Rusalka during Vidino divná (wonderful vision) from Dvořák's Rusalka during the final evening of the BBC Proms.

He followed Scotch Snap with Sit Down, You're the Rockin' the Boat - a famous show tune from the Broadway musical Guys and Dolls.

Spence went on to kick off the final stretch with Rule Britannia!

He received applause for his fourth costume of the evening - a jacket and kilt combo, featuring the Loch Ness Monster.

The evening concluded with a tribute to Dolly Parton, God Save the King and Auld Lang Syne.

articles.title: Northern Ireland consumers face rising energy prices
articles.summary: Iran war continues having an impact on people in Northern Ireland as energy prices climb again.
articles.body:
President Trump's comments on Ireland's possible constitutional future grabbed the headlines at the weekend.

But it is his war on Iran which is having a practical impact on people across the island as energy prices climb again.

A barrel of oil, on the widely used Brent crude measurement, has started this week at $108.

That is a four-month high and close to the level reached in the early stage of the conflict, when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz and reduced the amount of oil reaching world markets.

Some oil tankers are now moving through that important sea route but the latest price rise reflects a new front in the conflict.

A pipeline from Saudi Arabia which carries oil overland to ports on the Red Sea has been damaged in a drone strike and is closed for repairs.

Anything which forces up the price of oil is felt more quickly in Northern Ireland than anywhere else in Europe due to its heavy reliance on home heating oil.

Around two thirds of NI households use home heating oil.

Unlike gas or electricity the heating oil market is unregulated, so global price rises are rapidly passed through to consumers.

The NI Consumer Council heating oil tracker shows this is happening.

It suggests that on Monday the average price of 500 litres was £542, up almost 10% from £495 a week ago.

That is still well below the recent peak of almost £630 reached in early April.

But it does mean that consumers are facing into autumn with heating oil prices roughly double what they were last year.

The consumer council data shows that 500 litres would have cost just £270 in early September 2025.

The Northern Ireland Executive is attempting to soften that blow - a scheme to give lower income households a £100 oil voucher opened for applications last week .

The rising oil price is also being reflected on garage forecourts.

Consumer council data shows that last week that the average price of a litre of diesel was £1.77, 10p more expensive than it had been during the summer.

Unleaded petrol cost on average £1.57 a litre, the highest it has been since the conflict began and back to a level last seen in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The wholesale price of natural gas in the UK has also returned to a level last seen in the winter of 2022.

If that price level is sustained the gas companies supplying NI consumers will eventually have to impose another round of price increase beyond those announced in recent weeks.

Gas is also the key fuel for generating electricity across the island of Ireland so prices are rising there too.

Last week electricity supplier Share Energy said its price would increase by almost 13% in October.

Its chief executive Damian Wilson told the BBC that the Irish markets are at the mercy of geopolitical shocks.

"At the moment we are so reliant on gas. Power stations on the island of Ireland are predominately using gas," he said.

"We have no real storage facilities so we are susceptible to geopolitical factors.

"Before the Ukraine war gas would have traded at around 20p or 30p a therm (unit). It's now at 190p."

articles.title: Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia asked for the meeting to be postponed, but Tehran says it will continue to seek a regionally backed bill.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Another attempt to clinch a deal between Iran and Oman to restore some traffic to the Strait of Hormuz has been set back by a lack of regional consensus on the future of the waterway.

Officials from Iran, Iraq and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations – minus objecting Bahrain – were scheduled to meet in Oman’s port city of Salalah on Monday to confer on new temporary routes in the Strait of Hormuz amid Tehran’s ongoing hot-and-cold war with the United States.

On Sunday night, the region’s officials announced the postponement of the meeting, without giving a new date. None of the stakeholders gave any indication that the postponement was directly linked to recent Houthi and Iraqi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia.

However, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Saudi objection was the reason for the postponement, without providing further details.

US media outlets Axios and CNN reported that Saudi Arabia had submitted amendments to the Iran-Oman proposal for Hormuz because it had concerns that the wording would establish a new status quo which would be unacceptable to Riyadh.

It comes days after Saudi Arabia shut down its critical East-West oil pipeline – the kingdom’s key route for energy exports – after drone attacks in the area originating from Iraq. US President Donald Trump said these attacks were likely conducted at Tehran’s behest.

Saudi Arabia has also faced repeated attacks by the Houthis, who took control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast over the weekend.

Hours after the Salalah meeting was postponed, the Saudi civil defence issued alerts for Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran in southern and western parts of the kingdom. The Houthis claimed to have fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military facilities in Khamis Mushait, in retaliation for air strikes across Yemen, which it blames on Saudi Arabia.

Iran has said it will engage with the US on the future of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war only if there are tangible moves to lift Washington’s naval blockade on the country and return to the June memorandum of understanding .

With continued disruptions to the passage of vessels through the strait, Iran has signalled that it intends to continue pursuing the bilateral agreement with Oman over Hormuz, which it said was finalised last month.

“In consultation with Oman, in the next step, we will make a decision on how to announce or register the agreement,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters during a weekly news conference on Monday.

When the two countries initially advanced the bilateral deal, Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of US talks with Iran.

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Tehran wants to use its leverage over Hormuz for regional legitimacy – and ultimately to pressure the US.

“The broader the regional buy-in, the harder it becomes for the US to dismiss the arrangement as an Iranian diktat,” he told Al Jazeera.

GCC states, suffering from a sharp decrease in energy receipts, want ships moving and their economies insulated from a war they neither started nor can end. But Vaez said Washington is unlikely to lift the blockade on Iran even if the region blesses the arrangement between Muscat and Tehran.

“[The US] will find it much harder to sustain a policy that its own partners increasingly see as perpetuating the crisis,” Vaez said

The Omani-Iranian planned agreement envisions temporary entry and exit routes for commercial vessels in the strait, with Tehran repeatedly stating that this would not mean that the Strait of Hormuz has reopened.

Iran and Oman are the only two countries with territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. The proposed inbound corridor reportedly goes through Iranian waters, while the outbound corridor mostly passes through Omani waters, with small parts still in Iranian territory.

During Monday’s scheduled meeting, Iran and Oman were supposed to share precise maps and discuss the details of the routes with GCC members Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait, and Iraq, which is outside the bloc. The deal could reportedly include voluntary tolls to fund navigation, environmental protection and search-and-rescue operations.

Bahrain, which has borne the brunt of Iranian attacks since the US-Israel war on Iran started at the end of February, said it would not participate in the forum since it would amount to “appeasement”. The Tasnim news outlet, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), claimed Israel pushed Bahrain to refuse participation.

The latest diplomatic movement comes after days of explosive developments in Yemen, when the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, essentially took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea after a lightning offensive against government forces.

Thomas Juneau, assistant professor in the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa, said the Houthi advances represent a significant gain for Iran. Its Yemeni allies’ position in the Red Sea offers Iran an important new bargaining chip in future negotiations with the US.

“The Houthis are not a simple arm of Iranian foreign policy. They operate largely based on their own interests, and do not take and execute Iranian commands,” he told Al Jazeera. “But Houthi and Iranian interests are largely, if not always fully, aligned. They cooperate closely on the basis of those shared interests.”

Juneau sees the ability for Iran and the Houthis to potentially partially block traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb – two of the world’s most crucial maritime bottlenecks – would give them tremendous influence over the global economy, and thus the US.

The Houthis are trying to seize the opportunity to “institutionalise the de facto reality of their veto on maritime traffic” in the southern Red Sea and replicate partial Iranian success in doing the same in the Strait of Hormuz, Juneau said.

Iran has stressed that their allies’ gains in the Red Sea cannot be separated from the Saudi-led blockade and attacks on Houthi areas in Yemen since 2015.

“We know very well that continued war between Islamic countries in the region only has one winner, and that winner is no one but the Zionist regime, which is after persisting tensions and conflict in our region and between Islamic countries,” Iranian spokesperson Baghaei said.

articles.title: Father and son jailed for dragging 'terrified' police officer along road
articles.summary: Douglas Mills, 58, and Douglas Mills Jnr, 32,  sped off in an Audi after PC Mark Smith approached them over a suspected drug deal
articles.body:
A father and son who attempted to murder a police officer by dragging him along a road have been jailed.

Douglas Mills, 58, and Douglas Mills Jnr, 32, sped off in an Audi after PC Mark Smith approached them over a suspected drug deal in Hamilton, South Lanarkshire, in August 2024.

Smith, 35, was partly pulled into the car by the pair as Mills Jnr drove off and then hauled along before being left in a heap on the ground.

The officer suffered extensive injuries - including a fractured skull and a significant traumatic brain injury - and fears he will never be able to return to frontline policing.

The pair were found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow and both sentenced to 17 years.

Jurors watched graphic footage of Smith tumbling down the road and being left badly hurt.

The emotional officer said he thought he would never see his family again.

Judge William Gallacher told the duo they had "engaged in a murderous attack" that left the officer with "irreversible injuries which will have a substantial long-term effect on him to carry out normal activities."

He added: "This was a concerted conjoint attack with each of you doing separate things and in all the circumstances I see no reason to distinguish the penalties upon you."

The judge also imposed indefinite non-harassment orders prohibiting the pair from contacting their victim in any way.

Two years on from the incident Smith, who gave evidence behind a screen, has yet to return to duty.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The court heard Smith and his colleague, PC Colin Harris, spotted the Audi and recognised Mills Jnr as the driver, having been at his home weeks earlier.

Jurors were told a man then crossed the road - apparently clutching cash - and went to the passenger side of the Audi before making off.

The constable said he shouted "loudly" that it was police as he approached the car, while in possession of his warrant card and radio.

He told prosecutor Michelle Brannagan: "It was all very instantaneous. I felt myself being pulled off my feet.

"As soon as it happened, the car began to move off at speed."

Asked if he knew who was responsible for "pulling" him into the Audi, Smith said it happened quickly, and he was taken by surprise.

He said: "I had no opportunity to balance myself. I was aware that my legs were outside the car.

"All I remember was blows to my head and, to be honest, panicking."

The officer recalled seeing the speedometer going up to 50mph "in a matter of seconds" and said the blows to his head were strong enough that he was afraid he would lose consciousness.

Smith said: "I thought there is no chance I am surviving here if I hit the road at this speed.

"I thought I am never going to see my family again.

"I remember the sensation of the air blowing around me...how truly terrifying that moment was."

Smith said his last memory before everything went "black" was the driver "almost looking happy".

The officer's next recollection was being rushed to hospital in an ambulance.

The court heard he suffered a serious traumatic brain injury, a significant skull fracture and a blood clot.

The PC also lost a large percentage of the skin from his back after landing on the road and is on a waiting list for ankle ligament reconstruction.

Smith, who now suffers from sensory overload and low energy, said he thinks of the incident every time he looks in the mirror.

Mills Jnr gave evidence and claimed the initial encounter was a "chance meeting" with a family friend.

He also said he thought the officer was a mystery assailant.

After the sentencing, Smith said the attack had a huge impact on him and his life.

He said: "I was more than fortunate to survive, but part of me did not survive that day.

"Part of me was lost and two years later, I have started to accept that I will never be the same again.

"My job was a huge part of my identity. I'm unsure of what the future holds for me, and I fear that I will never be able to return to frontline policing."

Assistant Chief Constable Wendy Middleton described the murder bid as "despicable".

She said: "Not only has this had an effect on Mark and his family, but it has also had an impact on his close colleagues on the shift and the wider organisation."

Det Insp Scott Robertson, senior investigating officer, said the father and son were "two very dangerous and callous individuals".

He added: "Let us be clear that violence towards police officers is a serious criminal offence and anyone who behaves in this way should be in no doubt that we will rigorously pursue them and ensure they are brought to justice."

articles.title: London musical cancelled after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey pull out
articles.summary: Sunday in the Park With George was supposed to make its debut next year at the Barbican.
articles.body:
The upcoming London revival of Sunday In The Park With George has been cancelled after A-listers Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey dropped out.

The Wicked stars had been due to reunite on stage in the Stephen Sondheim show at the Barbican next year.

Last month, Grande announced she was pulling out of the musical as part of her decision to take a break from the spotlight after completing her Eternal Sunshine Tour.

Earlier this month, Bailey also revealed he was withdrawing from the show. Production company Empire Street Productions initially said it would continue as planned but on Monday announced the musical would no longer be staged in 2027.

A statement from the company said: "The planned 2027 production of Sunday in the Park with George at the Barbican will no longer proceed as scheduled.

"Empire Street Productions will retain the rights with a view to presenting the production in 2028. Further details will be announced in due course."

US composer Sondheim and playwright James Lapine created the original musical, which debuted on Broadway in 1984.

Sunday in the Park with George was inspired by French painter Georges Seurat's A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, in which a fictional version of the artist is consumed by his work.

Grande and Bailey played Glinda and Fiyero in the film adaptation of Wicked and its sequel, Wicked: For Good.

Grande's publicist announced in August that the singer and actress would be "taking a step back from visibility" after her recent tour ended.

A representative for the US star told People magazine that she "will be taking a step back from visibility" when the tour ends, after her appearances led to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

Grande's physical appearance and health have been a topic of speculation in recent years.

She later told fans at a Chicago concert: "The announcement that was made yesterday was not a reactive or impulsive thing. It is something that I had decided to plan... quietly, a long time ago."

"I heard my fans were worried negativity was ruining things for me but... that could not be more than the opposite.

"Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes."

When Bailey pulled out of Sunday in the Park with George at the beginning of September, he voiced support for its director Marianne Elliott and said: "I so look forward to seeing what the team, and the two actors who will now take on these roles, will create with it," he continued.

"I wish the very best to the entire company. I will be cheering them on as they continue with this production."

Bailey previously collaborated with Elliot on the play Cock and Sondheim's musical Company in the West End.

articles.title: Formula One set to make late call on Middle East season finale amid Iran war concerns
articles.summary: The last two rounds of the season are currently due to take place in the Middle East
articles.body:
Formula One is prepared to wait before deciding whether the current season can conclude in the Middle East .

The championship is scheduled to finish with consecutive rounds in Qatar on 29 November and Abu Dhabi a week later.

Imola has been put on standby to host the season finale if the Middle Eastern races cannot go ahead due to the United States- Iran conflict.

A decision finalising the status of the remaining races had been anticipated by the middle of this month.

However, it is understood there is no fixed timeline or hard deadline in place, and tickets for both events remain on sale.

Next year's calendar is expected to be announced later this week, potentially on Wednesday, with Bahrain and Saudi Arabia positioned to host the opening two rounds in March.

Both events were cancelled this year amid escalating violence in the region, though an unusual 'Bahrain Grand Prix' will take place next month at Malaysia's Sepang circuit, south of Kuala Lumpur.

Clear anxiety remains around holding a major global sporting event in the Middle East.

Current Foreign Office advice from the UK states that the "situation remains unpredictable" and warns of "a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation", though it no longer advises against travel to the region.

With Qatar and Abu Dhabi still officially listed on this year's schedule, nine rounds remain.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli took a significant step towards securing his first world title with victory in Madrid on Sunday.

The Italian benefitted from a Virtual Safety Car period that shattered Lando Norris' hopes of a third win in four races, virtually ending his outside chance of defending his world crown.

Norris labelled the VSC a "stupid rule" and demanded adjustments to the timing of its deployment to ensure fairness for drivers.

Four-time world champion Max Verstappen expects the issue to be discussed at the next drivers' briefing in Azerbaijan in two weeks.

He said: "It is extremely painful for Lando to lose a win. Sometimes you might lose points (because of the VSC) but this time it cost him a win.

"That's not nice, but a lot of drivers have had it in the past. Can it be better? Probably yes. We will talk about it in the next briefing and see if there is anything that can be done."

articles.title: ICE arrests Indian truck driver who overstayed in US for more than 8 years
articles.summary: US News: An Indian truck driver, Satvir Singh, was arrested by ICE in New Hampshire for overstaying his visa for more than eight years. This operation highlights ongoing enforcement actions in the U.S. immigration system.
articles.body: US immigration authorities arrested an Indian national who had remained in the country illegally for more than eight years during an enforcement operation at a commercial vehicle inspection station in New Hampshire.Satvir Singh was taken into custody by ICE Boston on September 11 at the inspection station in Hillsborough, where he was working as a truck driver involved in interstate commerce. He had a residence in New Jersey.Singh entered the US legally in 2017 but later violated the conditions of his admission by remaining in the country beyond the period allowed.The arrest was made during targeted operations at the Hillsborough inspection site, according to ICE Boston.The case comes less than two weeks after ICE Boston arrested another Indian national, Bankim Ramjibhai Aghera, in Keene, New Hampshire. Aghera had pending felony charges including aggravated sexual assault involving serious injury and sexual assault without consent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
